sources.title: How Pieter Levels ships 40+ solo startups: fast validation, simple PHP stack, automation
sources.originalTitle: Pieter Levels: Programming, Viral AI Startups, and Digital Nomad Life | Lex Fridman Podcast #440
sources.summary: Pieter Levels explains his scrappy solo-founder method: launch a micro-startup within weeks, charge from day one via Stripe, use the tech you already know, and automate everything with cron jobs. He walks through Photo AI, Nomad List, Hoodmaps and RemoteOK, plus views on frameworks, free users, exits and staying small.

principles.text: Launch a mini startup within about two weeks and check whether people actually pay, not just sign up.
principles.quote: I launch it very quickly, like within two weeks or something of building it, and I check if there's demand. And if people actually sign up, and not just sign up, but if people actually pay money

principles.text: Build with the tech you already know; stack matters less than validating that people will pay.
principles.quote: The tech stack is not actually, it's not the most important of a business when you're starting on a business. The important thing is that you validate that there's a market

principles.text: Skip free users; ask for money immediately and charge well above $10 as an indie.
principles.quote: I think free users generally don't convert. And I think if you have VC funding, it makes sense to get free users... I think it's best to start and just start asking people for money in the beginning.

principles.text: Do things manually first; constraints force you to automate only after demand is proven.
principles.quote: So the first few hundred, I just literally took their photos, train them, and then I would generate the photos with the prompts... But that's another constraint. I was forced to code something up that would do that.

principles.text: Automate operations with cron jobs, health checks and error alerts instead of hiring or managing people.
principles.quote: I log into the server and I do like sudo crontab-e... And that's how all my websites work.

principles.text: Use real users to A/B test model parameters, since their favorites and downloads reveal what works.
principles.quote: Just use the users to improve themselves. And I tell them when they sign up, we do sampling, we do testing on your photos of random parameters, and that worked really well.

sources.title: How Pieter Levels runs ~$3M/yr of automated indie sites solo with open revenue stats
sources.originalTitle: This Is What Real Freedom Looks Like - Pieter Levels
sources.summary: Levels explains how he runs Nomad List, Remote OK and other sites with one part-time contractor team, a deliberately simple PHP/jQuery stack, near-total automation and public revenue stats. He argues a $20k/month app is already a ~$1M asset, explains why he won't sell or raise VC, and credits radical transparency as a recurring marketing machine.

principles.text: Pick whatever stack gives the fastest feedback loop; it matters more than the tech.
principles.quote: it doesn't matter what you use, but as long as you use something that's really fast um, feedback loop and iterative loop where you can really quickly develop.

principles.text: Fast shipping makes customers happy because they see their feedback become product.
principles.quote: if you want happy customers, that's how you get it. You make something for them. They're like, "Oh my god, I influenced this product."

principles.text: A $20k/month app is already roughly a $1M asset, a far more reachable goal than a unicorn.
principles.quote: it's reachable, especially if you think about high automation, very high margins.

principles.text: Keep margins high with automation and part-time contractors instead of hiring a big team.
principles.quote: you work with part-time contracts like I do and you keep your margins very, very high because then you can sell for five x

principles.text: Even high-ticket sales can be fully automated via a self-serve Stripe checkout with a bundle slider.
principles.quote: I sell job post bundles for like 50k via stripe.

principles.text: Publishing open numbers and ups and downs is a recurring marketing machine that fuels audience and growth.
principles.quote: it's this recurring marketing machine that I think it's a big part of why my business is work became successful and why I got a lot of audience on Twitter

sources.title: How Pieter Levels bootstraps startups without funding: idea, launch, monetize, automate, exit
sources.originalTitle: How to Build a Startup Without Funding by Pieter Levels @ Dojo Bali
sources.summary: Levels shares the repeatable loop he found after launching many bootstrapped projects: solve your own problem, build fast alone, launch on Product Hunt/Hacker News/Reddit, grow organically, charge early, automate with scripts, then exit or move on. He stresses shipping small, validating with money, and avoiding paid or bot growth.

principles.text: Build products that solve your own problems; you are the expert and that is a competitive advantage.
principles.quote: when you have a problem you solve you're actually you were the expert at your own problems so this is an expert and you actually it's a competitive advantage

principles.text: Start with a small niche problem, make money, then grow the niche outward.
principles.quote: you have to start with something very small so if you look at Elon Musk he started with like PayPal which was a payment app for Palm Pilots

principles.text: Build solo and share your ideas freely; execution matters, not secrecy, and groupthink hurts.
principles.quote: nobody's gonna steal your idea it's all about execution everybody has the same ideas anyway it's the execution makes it original and unique

principles.text: Keep prototypes to about a month and launch to validate rather than polishing for months.
principles.quote: I would say max one month for a prototype it has to be a good prototype though but don't spend too much time working on something because you need to validate with launching

principles.text: Prefer organic growth over bots or paid traffic; it proves the product is actually good.
principles.quote: organic Grove is much cooler because it's much more hard to get but when you get it means you validated the product you built

principles.text: Charge money early and validate with buy buttons, even fake ones, before building features.
principles.quote: put buy buttons on everything it's the most important size my presentation you want to check what people pay for in your products

sources.title: Pieter Levels on why indie hacking got mainstream, AI startup moats, and validating before coding
sources.originalTitle: Pieter Levels — Indie Hacking is Dead. Now what?
sources.summary: Levels explains why indie hacking is now crowded and competes with funded companies, and how that plays out in AI startups where there is no moat, thin margins and supplier risk. He shares how he validates ideas manually with a landing page and payment link, and why he favors simple, old tech and going where the herd isn't.

principles.text: Once a path is mainstream, it gets crowded, so go where the herd isn't and stay there for years.
principles.quote: you should always do the opposite everybody else is doing so now if IND inding is mainstream you should probably like do something completely different you know what I mean like you should go where nobody's going

principles.text: Validate manually before coding: a landing page, a payment link and hand-done fulfillment beat building software first.
principles.quote: it was just a index of HTML actually was just a page with have examples of the avatars you could generate and the input photos and then link to type form no stripe checkout stripe payment link that was it

principles.text: Don't automate until the thing works; automation can cost more time than doing it by hand.
principles.quote: the time it takes to automate something is higher than the time that the thing takes so if that's true just do it yourself manually

principles.text: Don't over-polish an unvalidated product; a fancy design signals time spent on the wrong thing.
principles.quote: if it's too fancy it means you spend too much time on design or you it's some VC starter that spent too much money on designers if it's the beginning if it's not validated yet

principles.text: Tech choice matters less than execution speed; old, proven tech and simple code let you ship faster than rivals.
principles.quote: doesn't matter what you use there's no need for this cultism with developers

principles.text: Avoid depending on a single supplier, since they can raise prices once they see your success; keep alternatives ready.
principles.quote: when they saw my tweets where I was sharing my Revenue uh that I was making so much money with this they said sorry we need to increase the price to $20 per training

sources.title: Pieter Levels on going solo: $3M/yr, 70 projects, no VC
sources.originalTitle: A Cheeky Pint with serial entrepreneur Pieter Levels (@levelsio)
sources.summary: Levels explains why he picked indie hacking over VC funding: validate first, avoid the go-big-or-bust trap, and keep small projects alive for years. He also covers replacing hires with GPT, building an audience by posting constantly, and relying on ChatGPT referrals because he dislikes SEO.

principles.text: Validate and get traction before scaling; don't burn money on a product with no users.
principles.quote: validate first and build a business first um and see if you get traction like get to 50K or 100K a month.

principles.text: Raising VC locks you into a go-big-or-bust outcome with long odds, while staying indie keeps a smaller win valuable.
principles.quote: the problem is if you're a founder and you raise money, you kind of need to go big or bust, right?

principles.text: Build small projects that solve your own problems; most won't land, a few will.
principles.quote: just making stuff making little like creative projects that I needed to solve my problems and then most of the times nobody else needed that yes problem solved but like a few times it worked

principles.text: Replace hires and management overhead with GPT automation (e.g. community moderation) so one person can run many projects.
principles.quote: I can either hire people or I can just use GPT API

principles.text: Distribution compounds from relentless posting: his audience came from years of daily tweeting, not just a good launch.
principles.quote: I also work really hard cuz I tweeted like I think 125,000 times over 10 years. So it's like 40 tweets a day.

principles.text: Keep old projects running; small, low-maintenance products can earn for a decade without code changes.
principles.quote: I try to keep a lot of them running. I like to keep the internet history existing.

sources.title: Bootstrapping side projects to profit: how Pieter Levels grew Nomad List solo to ~$500K/year
sources.originalTitle: Bootstrapping Side Projects To Profit by Pieter Levels, Nomad List Founder
sources.summary: Pieter Levels walks through his 12 startups in 12 months experiment and how Nomad List grew without funding, events or paid marketing. He lays out five stages (idea, build, launch, grow, monetize) and argues for solo building, repeated launches, organic growth and charging from day one.

principles.text: Build for your own problems; you're the best first customer.
principles.quote: you're the expert on your own problems like you can figure out what to make you're the best customer for that product if you make it for yourself

principles.text: Start with a small niche and a story hook, then expand the niche later.
principles.quote: start small first so you can get bigger later because if you want to compete with big companies on the first day it's not going to work

principles.text: Build it yourself and work alone early to keep the feedback loop instant.
principles.quote: you need to have this fast feedback loop where you so if you do yourself like literally I make change like I wake up and I make the button green and that's my work like takes five seconds

principles.text: Validate with a buy button before building the real payment flow.
principles.quote: if you build MVP at a buy button it's so important you know see what people will pay for and the buy button doesn't even have to work

principles.text: Keep relaunching: ship new features and spin-offs every few months and pitch each as a story.
principles.quote: instead of launching one time you launch like every few months you have a new feature you launch it uh send send it to the press send it to all the big reddits

principles.text: Charge from the start and skip paid traffic so you learn if people truly want it.
principles.quote: charge early on and don't be don't be so afraid to charge it's so important

sources.originalTitle: The Future Of Marketing - Pieter Levels, Marc Köhlbrugge, Jim Groenen & David Arnoux Discuss

principles.text: Products start from a vividly visualized future vision that you already carry inside you, then get built in small steps.
principles.quote: you don't need search for vision it's already in you you just have to you know dig into yourself

principles.text: Rely on intuition and feel for your product more than analytics and endless A/B testing.
principles.quote: I don't really trust it I think you should go for your intuition like have a feeling about your product and how you would use it

principles.text: Over-optimizing conversion can win sales but leave customers who feel tricked; aim for happy customers, not maximal extraction.
principles.quote: you don't need to be you know optimize everything - it's not all about sales dude it's about having fun

principles.text: Press works as a sustained channel, but only if a good product backs it; old articles keep sending traffic.
principles.quote: you need to have a product that actually backs it because people want to read something and then they go to your product and if it sucks they're you know they're not going to care

principles.text: Paid retargeting was not worth it for him; he stays distrustful of it after testing.
principles.quote: I tried retargeting and I spent like two thousand dollars on Facebook

sources.summary: Four-hour AMA where Levels explains why scrappy, ugly products win, why he avoids VC and ads, and how he prices Nomad List and Remote OK. He covers error reporting via Telegram, lifetime pricing vs churn, motivation hacks, and building communities.

principles.text: Ship an ugly first version; early Google also looked bad, and polish isn't what customers pay for.
principles.quote: if you look at the first page of the first version of Google, it also looks shit. So all the first versions look shit.

sources.title: Pieter Levels on bootstrapping, spotting fringe markets early, and launching Rebase
sources.originalTitle: Interviewing Pieter Levels about his success and indie lifestyle
sources.summary: Levels explains how he picks markets by spotting fringe behavior that many people secretly want, why he ships many projects expecting most to fail, and why launches must fit each platform. He also covers starting with a side gig and living cheaply to extend runway, plus how Rebase (Portugal immigration) took off.

principles.text: Build where many people secretly want the same thing but nobody is doing or saying it yet; look for fringe behavior.
principles.quote: you want to be in the time where a lot of people are are secretly thinking the same thing

principles.text: Most projects fail, so ship many; expect only a few to work.
principles.quote: i've launched over 70 products projects and they you know only three or four or something worked out so most of the times you're wrong

principles.text: Tailor each launch to the platform. On Reddit, give value as a community member instead of announcing.
principles.quote: reddit is completely anti-spam so the only thing the only way to leverage reddit is to be to give value like to be a beneficial community member

principles.text: Nobody cares that you launched a startup, so shipping is a reality check that the product must be better or cheaper.
principles.quote: nobody cares it's not interesting it's it's annoying it looks like spam

principles.text: Start with a side gig or existing income rather than quitting outright, so you don't run out of money.
principles.quote: i think 100 side gig i mean i did the same thing

principles.text: Use location freedom to live somewhere cheap, which stretches your runway.
principles.quote: it is a really a really good trick is to to use this uh freedom to go live in a cheap place

sources.title: How Pieter Levels built 12 startups in 12 months to ship fast and earn press
sources.originalTitle: Interview: Pieter Levels of Levels.io on How to Pull Off 12 (Well Executed) Startups in 12...
sources.summary: Levels explains why he builds one minimal MVP per month after a two-year project flopped with four free trial users. The monthly deadline forces him to finish and keep scope small, and the 12-in-12 narrative earns press coverage that drives users. He also covers sourcing ideas from his own problems, funding bigger goals with side-project cash flow, and not being intimidated by polished products.

principles.text: Ship small products fast; a monthly deadline forces you to finish and keep scope minimal.
principles.quote: if I have to build something every month it forced me to finish it and it forced me to keep it minimal as well which I think is a good in terms of an MVP right

principles.text: Long perfectionist builds often launch to nobody; shorten the loop to learn demand sooner.
principles.quote: after like two years I launched it and nobody was using it there was just like there's like four free trial users using it and they left

principles.text: Press wants news; build a narrative around your products or personality that fits you, and use press to get users.
principles.quote: you need to think of a narrative around your products or around your personality I guess um that fits your personality as well because you you can't fake it right

principles.text: Build products that solve a problem you have yourself, and borrow proven layouts for inspiration.
principles.quote: I get an ID from probably some problem I have myself like with Nomad list I had the problem where I didn't really know which cities to go to

principles.text: Ideas are common; execution is what differentiates, so keep a backlog and ship.
principles.quote: I think we all have the same ideas and it's just about execution now

principles.text: Use side projects for monthly cash flow to fund working on bigger problems later.
principles.quote: you need cash flow to solve big problems right most of the times so if you if you're in a nine-to-five job and you want to solve big problems I guess a good Avenue would be to build your own stuff that gives you cash flow monthly

sources.title: How Pieter Levels runs a solo app portfolio: scrappy shipping, vanilla PHP and AI-assisted code
sources.originalTitle: 40 - Network State Conference 2024 - Fireside with Pieter Levels and Balaji
sources.summary: In a fireside with Balaji, Pieter Levels explains how he maintains Nomad List, Photo AI and other apps nearly alone. He favors scrappy, fast shipping on a stable vanilla PHP stack, with AI coding help, and builds features that solve real nomad pain. The rest of the talk covers digital nomad stats and network state debate.

principles.text: Keep things scrappy and ship fast, but never cut corners on security when you hold user data.
principles.quote: generally uh I like to keep it Scrappy and like to ship fast

principles.text: Pick a boring, stable stack (vanilla PHP) so little changes and maintenance stays low; improve it slowly.
principles.quote: because it's PHP and it's vanilla cult um nothing really changes

principles.text: Lean on AI coding tools like Cursor to write more of the code as a solo builder.
principles.quote: I use cursor a lot like I use a lot of AI stuff now to write codes

principles.text: Data-heavy products can be cheap to maintain: refresh from public sources on a yearly cadence.
principles.quote: you don't need to update a lot like you update every year for example you get new data from World bank right or IMF

principles.text: Build proactive features that solve a painful, specific problem, like tax-liability alerts for travelers.
principles.quote: I send my robot sends you a message if you uh become tax liable in the next 30 days in a country because you add your Trips N list

principles.text: Mine your own user base for data to understand your audience and publish it as a feature.
principles.quote: I have all these users and they do a lot of things they talk to each other they do meetups um and I have one statistics page

sources.title: Pieter Levels on how digital nomadism evolved and where network states fit
sources.originalTitle: Pieter Levels Interviewed by Sondre Rasch
sources.summary: In a short fireside chat at SafetyWing's summit, Levels recounts how timing and circumstance (faster internet, a Dutch graduate priced out of Holland) led him into nomad startups. He argues the nomad niche has split into subgroups as its users age, that European institutions and startups are too slow, and that the opportunity now lies in services for settled, relocating people.

principles.text: Big opportunities often appear when a technology shift meets your personal situation at the right moment.
principles.quote: there was this time where there was a technological possibility of people working on a laptop from the other side of the world. And there was me, graduating university, wanting to get out of Holland and Europe and uh building a startup

principles.text: Write and tweet publicly about a new niche early; it reaches early adopters in the developer world.
principles.quote: I was writing about it. I was blogging about it. You know, how many I was tweeting about it. And it started to get um into the the technological programmer developer world

principles.text: Markets mature by fragmenting: one niche splits into many subgroups with distinct needs.
principles.quote: it was one niche group. And now it's kind of split into a lot of different groups.

principles.text: Your original audience ages and its needs change, so build for its next life stage.
principles.quote: the people that were like 25 back then are now 35. You know, many of them have kids and families.

principles.text: Complaining is not enough; take action by posting solutions and crowdsourcing ideas publicly.
principles.quote: You can complain about that. You know, what we were doing, we complain a lot. But then you also need to start taking action. So, I started tweeting about like solutions and I started crowdsourcing ideas

principles.text: Services helping people relocate and settle abroad are a big market worth building for.
principles.quote: there's a lot of companies that are trying to help people migrate now. And that's a big market. Like, if you want to jump in there, for sure.

sources.title: Pieter Levels on remote work, bootstrapping, and finding meaning as a nomad
sources.originalTitle: How Remote Work Will Let Millions of People Relocate
sources.summary: Pieter Levels talks with SafetyWing's Sondre about how remote work is going mainstream, why he stays bootstrapped, and why meaning comes from people rather than aesthetics. He explains how Nomad List started as a fix for his own problem and which problems remote workers still need solved.

principles.text: Build products by solving your own problem; Nomad List began as his own need to find the next city.
principles.quote: It was more of a solving my own problem because back then I was nomading a lot more rapidly than now

principles.text: Bootstrapping keeps you wired to the market: revenue shows instantly whether a change works.
principles.quote: because it's bootstrapped, you're so tapped into the market as a signal where anything you do to your startup or website, you immediately see if it works or not because you make money on it or not.

principles.text: VC money blurs market feedback and removes the incentive to build revenue; odds of an exit are low without an unfair advantage.
principles.quote: And with venture capital, you have all this money in your bank account, you know, you can spend it on all these things and there's not a lot of incentive, especially in the beginning, to, you know, build revenue or profit.

principles.text: Fringe ideas can become mainstream; early pushback reflects culture, not arguments, so keep pushing, then look for the next fringe.
principles.quote: every fringe subculture has potential to become mainstream because usually you're an early adopter that's to something that will absolutely not be accepted in the beginning by mainstream society.

principles.text: Half-remote companies break culturally; be fully in-office or fully remote.
principles.quote: it's very difficult to have companies that are half remote where like some people from the team work remotely and some people stay in the office.

principles.text: Improve existing places and communities rather than trying to build new villages from scratch.
principles.quote: instead of trying to create new villages, which reinvent the whole concept of society, try to iterate on the society you're currently living in.

sources.title: How to build a bootstrapped startup without funding: Levels' 10-step list
sources.originalTitle: How to build a bootstrapped startup without funding — @levelsio (Pieter Levels)
sources.summary: Pieter Levels lays out a 10-point playbook for building a startup with no funding: solve your own problem, ship ugly fast, charge from day 1, use boring tech and cheap hosting, do support yourself, automate, build in public, and keep burn near zero. He frames VC as a game that makes founders think they need permission.

principles.text: Build for a problem you personally have and use your product daily.
principles.quote: pick a problem you personally have. if you don't use your own product daily, quit now

principles.text: Skip the pitch deck and ship something ugly in a weekend.
principles.quote: skip the pitch deck. open your code editor. ship something ugly in a weekend

principles.text: Charge money from day 1; free users mostly create support burden.
principles.quote: charge money from day 1. free users give you nothing but support tickets

principles.text: Use boring tech and cheap hosting; avoid frameworks and heavy infrastructure.
principles.quote: use boring tech. PHP, SQLite, vanilla JS. frameworks are a trap that mass waste your time

principles.text: Do customer support yourself as your fastest product feedback loop.
principles.quote: do customer support yourself. it's the fastest product feedback loop that exists

principles.text: Grow by building in public; your journey is the marketing.
principles.quote: grow on Twitter/X by building in public. your journey IS the marketing

sources.title: How Pieter Levels builds MVPs fast: rough, minimal, own-stack shipping
sources.originalTitle: How I build my minimum viable products — @levelsio (Pieter Levels)
sources.summary: Levels explains his 12-startups workflow: solve your own problems, keep sites minimal, own the whole stack on one cheap VPS, skip frameworks and databases, and deploy a new site in about 15 minutes. His core message is that tools matter less than being fast and comfortable with what you know.

principles.text: Start by solving your own problems; it's a great way to begin, even if you later aim for a wider audience.
principles.quote: It’s great to start off by solving your own problems.

principles.text: Build minimal on purpose; don't build big immediately or stuff a site with functionality.
principles.quote: I don’t have as much as time to build things big and I don’t see the point of building things big immediately.

principles.text: Work fast and rough rather than longer hours; speed comes from workflow, not hours.
principles.quote: I don’t work particularly longer hours than most people (I think). I do work fast and rough.

principles.text: Avoid frameworks that add complexity; keep code simple and reuse code from previous projects.
principles.quote: Except for jQuery, I don’t use any frameworks. Why? Because many times, they just make things more complex.

principles.text: Own the whole stack on one simple, cheap server so you can debug quickly and deploy in minutes.
principles.quote: I now owned the entire stack. From front-end, back-end to the server itself.

principles.text: Use plain JSON files instead of a database at small scale; migrate to a real database later if needed.
principles.quote: You can always write a script that puts this in a MySQL/MariaDB/PostgreSQL database later.

sources.title: Why Pieter Levels launched 12 startups in 12 months: finish and ship small
sources.originalTitle: I'm Launching 12 Startups in 12 Months — @levelsio (Pieter Levels)
sources.summary: Levels explains his 2014 challenge to launch one startup per month. He diagnoses creatives' two killers, not finishing and fear of launching, and argues for starting small, exposing yourself to market forces, and defining a startup as a new product that grows fast.

principles.text: Forcing yourself to ship on a fixed cadence beats perfectionism; finishing and launching are the real bottlenecks, not building.
principles.quote: I can already build stuff. My challenge is to actually finish and launch my projects. So for the next 12 months, I’ve set the goal to launch 12 startups in 12 months.

principles.text: Fear of failure makes builders under-launch or never launch because they compare reality to a fantasy launch.
principles.quote: The fear of failure takes over so we don’t put enough effort into launching or we don’t launch at all.

principles.text: Start small instead of waiting for a big vision; the big vision comes after market fit with an MVP.
principles.quote: The big vision happened after they found a market fit with their MVPs.

principles.text: Taking action beats idle planning; you learn by exposing yourself to the market, even if you do the wrong thing first.
principles.quote: You’ll figure out what you need to do by exposing yourself to the world (and its market forces). And especially if you’re not experienced like me, I think it’s better to start small first, and slowly build bigger things.

principles.text: A startup is a new product that grows fast; building is easy, growing is hard.
principles.quote: Delivering a new product is the easy part, growing it fast is the hard part.

principles.text: Time-box validation: if a product shows no demand within a month of launching the MVP, treat it as failed and move on.
principles.quote: My plan is to see if I can get market fit in one month, and if it doesn’t show any signs of being somewhat in demand, I consider it failed.

sources.title: Only 4 out of 70+ projects made money: ship more because hit rate is ~5%
sources.originalTitle: Only 4 out of 70+ projects I ever did made money and grew — @levelsio (Pieter Levels)
sources.summary: Pieter Levels shares that only 4 of his 70+ projects ever made money and grew, meaning over 95% failed. His takeaway is that a ~5% hit rate is normal, so the way to win is to ship many projects.

principles.text: Expect most projects to fail; a ~5% hit rate is normal even for a successful maker.
principles.quote: 📉 >95% of everything I ever did failed

principles.text: Since hit rate is low, the answer is to ship more projects to get more chances at a winner.
principles.quote:
📈 My hit rate is only about ~5%

🚀 So...ship more

principles.text: Only a handful of many attempts end up making money and growing; success is concentrated in few projects.
principles.quote: Only 4 out of 70+ projects I ever did made money and grew

sources.title: How Pieter Levels hit $1M annual revenue in 4 years with Nomad List and Remote OK
sources.originalTitle: It took 4 years to reach $1m annual revenue with Nomad List and Remote OK — @levelsio (Pieter Levels)

principles.text: Build slowly and profitably: $1M/yr took 4 years, with no funding and no ad budget.
principles.quote: It took 4 years to get here, but we did it:

principles.text: Grow without paid acquisition or outside money; revenue can come from the products themselves.
principles.quote:
🎫 0 ad budget 
💰 0 funding

principles.text: Keep infrastructure lean: two apps on a single server, heavily automated with cron jobs.
principles.quote: 🤖 208 cron jobs

principles.text: A small portfolio of products can add up: two apps together reached $1M annualized.
principles.quote: 💎 2 apps: [nomadlist.com](https://nomadlist.com) + [remoteok.io](http://remoteok.io)

sources.title: How Pieter Levels hit $10M/y in revenue and gains at a 94.5% profit margin
sources.originalTitle: I passed $10M/y in revenue and investment gains with a 94.5% profit margin — @levelsio (Pieter Levels)
sources.summary: Levels explains how relentlessly cutting costs, including replacing SaaS tools by vibecoding his own, produced a 94.5% profit margin. The savings were invested in ETFs and a few startup bets, so investment returns now exceed his stable $200K-$250K/mo business revenue.

principles.text: Aggressively push profit margin as high as possible by cutting costs and SaaS dependencies.
principles.quote: I've always been aggressively increasing my profit margins to as high as possible, especially the last few years, and especially this year where I've reduced my SaaS dependencies to just a handful of companies by vibecoding my own replacements

principles.text: Lower costs compound: more profit becomes savings, then investments, then returns.
principles.quote: Spend less -> lower costs -> more profit -> more money saved -> more money to invest -> more % returns on investments

principles.text: Invest surplus mostly in simple index ETFs, with a few opportunistic bets in companies you use and see demand for.
principles.quote: Most of my investments have been simple ETFs like Vanguard S&P500, but also a few lucky stock and startup bets that worked out

principles.text: Ask the services you depend on whether you can invest in them; you know their value firsthand.
principles.quote: From then I just asked every app/service I used if I could invest, like @cursor_ai in 2025

principles.text: Lean, profitable, healthy growth beats spending everything to grow, even if the company ends up smaller.
principles.quote: Many people in the last decade told me to spend all my money, either personally or with my business to grow it, we don't know how that would have ended up, maybe my companies would be bigger, but I'm happy I did it in my own lean profitable healthy way

principles.text: Track profit margin and health (sleep) metrics together as equally important.
principles.quote: I keep my revenue/gains together with my profit margin and my sleep score in my situation monitor dashboard, as those are equally important :D

sources.title: How Pieter Levels built the #nomads Slack community around Nomad List
sources.originalTitle: How to successfully build a community around your startup — @levelsio (Pieter Levels)
sources.summary: Levels explains why press spikes decay and how a loosely branded community keeps users coming back. He seeded a Slack chat with authorities, rolled it out gradually, launched publicly, and hit 300+ members in 24 hours. The community doubles as a user focus group, launch channel and marketing engine.

principles.text: Getting users is harder than building; press spikes decay, so build a community to keep bringing people back.
principles.quote: The hardest part of startups these days is not building the product or app. It’s getting people to actually use what you built.

principles.text: A community sticks far longer than press coverage and can be turned into users for any product you push next.
principles.quote: The advantage to a community is that it sticks a lot longer than press coverage.

principles.text: A community can be informal and only loosely tied to your brand; it need not be a forum or on your own site.
principles.quote: A community doesn’t have to be completely tied to your brand.

principles.text: Seed a community top-down with respected authorities, test privately, then roll out gradually to keep quality high.
principles.quote: To make sure the community was of value, I used a top-down approach where I first invited other people that were authorities in the remote community already

principles.text: A community is a free focus group: see problems, ask what to build, and launch new products straight to it.
principles.quote: It’s a free user focus group.

principles.text: Add a price to cap growth and keep out spammers as the community grows.
principles.quote: To put an artificial limit on the chat’s growth and keep these people out, I’ve added a $15 to $25 price

sources.title: Make a great product: why a great product pushes itself
sources.originalTitle: Make a great product — @levelsio (Pieter Levels)
sources.summary: Levels reflects on self-releasing his 2008 drum & bass album, building and marketing everything himself. He concludes that marketing can take you far, but time is better spent making the product great, and that gatekeepers and tastemakers still matter.

principles.text: A truly great product pushes itself; invest in quality before marketing.
principles.quote: Make a great product. Chances are it will push itself before you even thought about marketing it.

principles.text: Time spent on promotion is often better spent making the product better.
principles.quote: if I had dedicated the time I spent on marketing and promoting it on making the music better I think it would have gone much further.

principles.text: You can market a product to success but cannot force people to like it.
principles.quote: you can market your music to success but you can not force people to like your music.

principles.text: You cannot do everything alone; you need tastemakers and respected people to push your name.
principles.quote: you cannot do everything on your own. And even if you can, you don’t want to. You are always going to need others

principles.text: Get really good first and don't self-release too early; significant people find good work.
principles.quote: don’t release your own stuff independently too early. Get really good at making music first.

principles.text: Self-marketing gets you far, but an absolutely great product pushes itself.
principles.quote: Marketing your product and putting it to the market yourself can get you far, but an absolutely great product pushes itself.

sources.title: VC vs bootstrapped startups: the emotional curve of each path
sources.originalTitle: VC startups vs bootstrapped startups — @levelsio (Pieter Levels)
sources.summary: A short emoji-based essay contrasting the emotional trajectories of VC-funded and bootstrapped startups. VC startups start with a rush of money and euphoria that ends in a crash, while bootstrapped startups start with doubt and struggle before ending in sustained happiness.

principles.text: VC-funded startups front-load the reward (money and excitement) and often end in a painful crash.
Bootstrapped startups back-load the reward: early doubt and struggle, then profit and lasting happiness.
principles.quote: Bootstrapped startups: 🤔🤓😮😧😵😞😒💰😏🙂😀😄😃😆😁

principles.text: Building startups without funding is a viable path worth pursuing.
principles.quote: I wrote a book called MAKE about building startups without funding.

sources.title: Founder dilution math: why ~5% is the typical final stake in VC-backed startups
sources.originalTitle: 5% ownership is probably the most common final stake for VC funded startup founders — @levelsio (Pieter Levels)
sources.summary: Levels uses Carta median data to show how each funding round and each co-founder shrinks a founder's stake, then converts that into expected payouts at a $1B exit, a median $71M exit, and probability-weighted outcomes. His point: VC is a moonshot game, and the typical founder ends with a small slice of a small exit.

principles.text: Funding is never free: every round sells a slice of the company, and you only win if the remaining part is worth more.
principles.quote: Raising money is not free, people don't give you money out of charity, they buy a little slice of your company every time they invest

principles.text: Dilution plus co-founders pushes the typical VC-backed founder's final stake down to around 5%.
principles.quote: ~5% ownership probably the most common final % most VC funded startups will have when they work out, especially when you have a co-founder

principles.text: Judge outcomes realistically: median exit values are far below the billion-dollar headline numbers.
principles.quote: the median acquisition value for a VC-backed startup sits at approximately $71 million

principles.text: Most startups never get acquired, so probability-weighted expected payouts are much smaller than the exit figures suggest.
principles.quote: most startups are by definition doomed to fail, only ~15% of startups ever get acquired

principles.text: VC is a high-variance path chosen for the rare huge payout, not a bad deal; know the math before taking it.
principles.quote: VC-backed startups shoot for the moon, it's one of the few ways you can have a crazy big payout and become an actual billionaire

principles.text: Bootstrapping with your own money makes billionaire-scale outcomes rare, but you keep ownership.
principles.quote: which is very rare as a bootstrapped founder with your own money!

sources.title: How Pieter Levels weighed a $45K offer for Go Fucking Do It and decided not to sell
sources.originalTitle: How I did not sell my startup today — @levelsio (Pieter Levels)
sources.summary: Levels received a $45K offer for his second 12-startups-in-12-months project after one month of work. He declined because the price didn't reflect the site's potential, he was still enjoying it, and he wants to build startups rather than cash out cheaply. He also lists his five goals for the experiment.

principles.text: Don't sell a startup for less than a strong multiple of the revenue it could generate once scaled.
principles.quote: If I can scale it up to 10x, it can generate double that offer in revenue annually. So it’d have to be a strong multiple of that before I I’d consider selling it.

principles.text: Keep a project while it still excites you; fresh enthusiasm is a reason not to sell.
principles.quote: I’m having way too much fun with it still. The whole concept and execution is still so fresh and doesn’t bore me yet.

principles.text: A quick payout that turns you into a well-paid freelancer defeats the purpose of building startups.
principles.quote: I’m trying to build startups here, not be just an expensive web developer (at EUR 16k/m).

principles.text: Account for taxes when evaluating an exit: a headline offer shrinks a lot after tax.
principles.quote: Now with Dutch tax grabbing 52% of that, I’d be left with about EUR 16,000.

principles.text: Define your goals: living standards via projects without a job, then investment or a sale that buys years of runway to build.
principles.quote: it’s being able to maintain my living standards with my projects without having to get a job.

principles.text: An unsolicited acquisition offer is a signal you may be onto something worth scaling.
principles.quote: It may show I’m on to something here that I can scale up…so let’s go fucking grow it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Pieter Levels explains his scrappy solo-founder method: launch a micro-startup within weeks, charge from day one via Stripe, use the tech you already know, and automate everything with cron jobs. He walks through Photo AI, Nomad List, Hoodmaps and RemoteOK, plus views on frameworks, free users, exits and staying small.

chunks.heading: Validate fast with a two-week build and a paid checkout
chunks.text:
- Pieter funds nothing with VC. He designs, codes, and launches everything alone, so he has to move fast to learn whether an idea works.
- He builds a mini startup and launches within about two weeks, then checks whether people actually pay with a credit card. Signups alone do not validate an idea.
- Most ideas fail. His response is statistical: try many cheap things and expect a few to work.
- His "12 Startups in 12 Months" project capped each product at one month, with a Stripe checkout button on each. He published the results publicly (Hacker News, a blog post) for accountability.
- The hard part of a 30-day build is deciding what not to build. His rule of thumb: landing page, Stripe, the core product, and a plan for how people will find it.
- Early login was a static link with a hash. Real Google login took about a year to add.
- He says big companies are slow because of bureaucracy and legal review. He cites Google, which had the transformer tech and the data but did not ship a ChatGPT-style product.

chunks.heading: Photo AI and AI avatars: from a Typeform and Stripe link to a fine-tuning product
chunks.text:
- **Path:** Stable Diffusion led to thishousedoesnotexist.org (houses), then interiorai.com (image-to-image interior redesign), then avatarai.me, then Photo AI (photorealistic photos without a photographer).
- **Interior AI:** It made $10K-20K a month within a week of launch. Pieter says it still makes about $40K-50K a month after two years.
- **Avatar launch (October 2022):**
  - He trained a model on his own face and tweeted the results.
  - Demand arrived by DM, so he made an HTML page with a Stripe payment link and a Typeform for photo uploads. There was no code behind it.
  - The first hundreds of orders were manual: download the zip, train the model, run prompts from a text file, and email results from his personal email.
  - The manual load forced him to build the real automated site.
  - He made about $100K in AI avatars and about $150K in a week, his biggest payout. He says it was "10K a day."
- **Competition:** A VC-backed studio (Lensa, which already had an app and user base) copied the feature and reportedly made about $30M. He called it a hype, and the cheesy art style was too easy for the AI to get away with. He pivoted to real photorealism.
- **Vendor risk:** His GPU vendor raised training prices from $3 to $20 once it saw his revenue, after he had been selling at $30. He moved his business to Replicate by DMing its CEO and asking for DreamBooth fine-tuning. He has trained about 36,000 models on it.
- **Training data tips:**
  - Whatever is constant across training photos (a green shirt) gets learned as part of the concept, so photos need diverse clothes, lighting, and locations.
  - He mixes full-body photos with face crops so body shape is kept.
  - Training data quality matters more than training time.
- **A/B testing on users:** With over a million photos a month, he randomly tested generation parameters (step count, sampler) on about 10% of users. He measured favorites and downloads, checked significance, then rolled the winner out to everyone. Users are told sampling happens.
- **Safety:** Photorealistic fine-tunes carry porn in their base. He prompts out nudity and runs Google Vision to check every image for NSFW before showing it, because journalists complain.
- **Honesty:** "AI startups all act like it's perfect," but results are hit or miss (about 50/50 early on), and people still sign up.

chunks.heading: Boring stack, instant deploys, and automation
chunks.text:
- **Stack:** Vanilla HTML/CSS, jQuery, PHP, SQLite. He says it was accidental, since he never found time to learn Node.js.
- **On frameworks:** He is suspicious of well-funded frameworks and hosting platforms that pay developer influencers. He asks "did you make money with it? Did you charge users?" He still says to use a framework if it solves a direct problem.
- **Tools:** The IDE is not important. He uses VS Code (previously Sublime Text). He builds with what he knows, and he can always rewrite later.
- **Deploy flow:** He edits CSS or PHP, presses Command+Enter, and it pushes to GitHub. A webhook then pulls to the server and it is live in about a second or two. He deploys straight to production with no staging server. PHP Lint and djLint catch errors.
- **Speed:** He had about 37,000 git commits in the last 12 months. He sometimes times himself fixing a user-reported bug in about two minutes.
- **Automation:**
  - Everything runs on cron jobs (`sudo crontab -e`, hourly PHP scripts).
  - Nomad List meetups are self-serve: a page to organize one, an automatic tweet, and DMs to nomads in that city. About 30 meetups a month with no effort from him.
- **Monitoring:**
  - A healthcheck.php page runs database checks (e.g. data sanity, signups in the last 24 hours) and prints a red X or green check.
  - UptimeRobot opens the page every minute and keyword-checks for the red X. Failures send an alert to Telegram.
  - Every JavaScript and PHP error is also sent to Telegram, which gets him toward zero errors.
- **AI moderation:** GPT-4 reviews Nomad List city reviews and moderates a chat of about 10,000 members. He is alerted only on rejections. He says it understands humor and double meanings.
- **Costs:** He keeps profit margins high and has no employees. He emails AI vendors for discounts, and 25-50% discounts are common.

chunks.heading: Nomad List, Hoodmaps and RemoteOK: start scrappy and let users build the data
chunks.text:
- **Nomad List:**
  - It began as a public, editable Google Sheet of cities with internet speed and cost of living, shared on Twitter.
  - It was then turned into a website. Seeing it go viral with few followers showed demand.
  - The rating is now mostly national public data sets (World Bank, UN). Crowdsourced ratings were skewed because some groups boosted their own country.
  - Members' check-ins still drive about half the ranking. The site has roughly 30,000-45,000 members and has run for almost ten years.
  - It is his baby, so he doesn't want to sell it.
- **Hoodmaps (built in about a week):**
  - Users draw colors on a map to label neighborhoods: tourist, hipster, rich, business, residential.
  - He used HTML5 canvas, normalized coordinates by removing decimals, and a cron job picks the most common color per cell.
  - He added tags with upvotes (his model came from Reddit).
  - Mapbox once billed him $20,000 after a viral spike, so he later moved to an open-source map platform.
  - It makes no money, and he says it is fine: "you don't need to monetize everything."
- **RemoteOK:** A spin-off from the Nomad List jobs page. At the 2021 peak it made about $140K a month from job posts, with $299 entry listings, upsells such as rainbow colors and background images, and a few $3,000-4,000 posts. It later fell to about $10K a month and is now back to about $40K.
- **Chrome extensions and plugins:** Pieter says people don't pay for plugins, so make an extension a feature of a product.

chunks.heading: Pricing, distribution, and feedback
chunks.text:
- **Charge from day one:** He says free users rarely convert and abuse AI apps heavily. Without VC money, he charges at once.
- **Price:** He recommends more than $10 a month, ideally $30 or more per user, since indie makers can't match Netflix scale. 1,000 users at $30 is $30K a month.
- **Community:** Paying users form a higher-quality group. A Discord with developers and users together is now normal.
- **Distribution:**
  - Organic wins. If you use Reddit, solve a specific problem for a subreddit rather than posting a startup pitch.
  - TikTok, Reels and X test content on a small group (about 300 people) and promote it by performance, not follower count.
  - One TikTok by a random creator added about $20,000 a month to Photo AI. Some AI influencers charge about $4,000 after a video goes viral.
- **Haters:** He treats haters as useful, because some have a point (hard signup, bad data). He has muted about 15,000 accounts, and he mutes rather than blocks.
- **Building in public:** He finds personal tweets more engaging than single-topic ones.

chunks.heading: Finding ideas, learning, and working habits
chunks.text:
- **Ideas:**
  - Note daily annoyances and travel arbitrage, such as WeChat-style super-apps seen in Asia.
  - He keeps ideas in Telegram saved messages and used Trello earlier.
  - Technology-first ideas, like Stable Diffusion, are riskier ("solution looking for a problem").
  - He thinks first ideas can be good because they come from subconscious processing.
- **Learning:** He learns by acting. He asks ChatGPT, copies the code, and tweaks it. Bootcamps do not work well, in his view. He says AI is a better use of time than a front-end framework.
- **Work style:**
  - One MacBook screen is enough. He is "suspicious of more," and he avoids gear acquisition syndrome.
  - Constraints make him happier than freedom. For new projects he wants uninterrupted time and sometimes pulls all-nighters.
  - He works with industrial techno and strong V60 coffee.
  - He uses a $1 fine per phrase spoken in 45-minute cowork sprints.
- **Team:** He rarely works with others. He is building an AI startup with friend Andre (Andre codes in Ruby; Pieter handles product direction and Twitter). He once hired a Python/AI developer for 10 months because he couldn't do Python.

chunks.heading: Exits and staying small
chunks.text:
- He has never sold a company. In acquisition talks, buyers dragged on for 6-12 months and then cut the price.
- His products have about 90% margins and run mostly automated. Selling at 3-5x profit or revenue is equivalent to waiting 3 years, so he doesn't sell below a high multiple. Only 6-8x would tempt him.
- He thinks AI products like Photo AI are easier to sell than Nomad List.
- He is wary of retirement and the emptiness after exits, so he prefers to keep building.
- Founders with large funding told him they would build like him next time because it is "more fun, more indie, more chill." They don't enjoy being managers.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Levels explains how he runs Nomad List, Remote OK and other sites with one part-time contractor team, a deliberately simple PHP/jQuery stack, near-total automation and public revenue stats. He argues a $20k/month app is already a ~$1M asset, explains why he won't sell or raise VC, and credits radical transparency as a recurring marketing machine.

chunks.heading: Pieter's one-person, contractor-based business model and numbers
chunks.text:
- Pieter runs several products as the only full-time person. His stated numbers in the interview:
  - Nomad List: past roughly 100K a month, close to a million dollar business. It showed a 73% profit margin on his public open page.
  - Remote OK (job board): about 1.6 million a year, his biggest earner, at about 94% pre-tax margin.
  - Rebase (immigration/relocation agency for remote workers): his newest business.
  - The ebook (Read Make): about 4K a month.
- His public revenue meter targets 3 million a year. The interviewers cited 2.7 million at the time.
- Team: a part-time customer support contractor who covers all projects, a Slack community moderator, and a devops friend on an SLA-style arrangement.
- The devops contractor gets alerted if a server goes down and handles security updates. Pieter says it "never goes down anymore."
- He argues moderation cannot be fully automated: "you need a real person there" because Slack communities have drama. He tried automating it first.
- He hosts on a VPS (DigitalOcean and Linode), not Amazon.
- He describes the sites as "heavily automated," roughly 99.9%, and says he barely needs to work on them.
- His reasoning for part-time contractors: keep margins very high, so revenue is almost profit, which is what makes a sale multiple worth it.

chunks.heading: Simple stack and fast feedback loop
chunks.text:
- Pieter builds with PHP, jQuery, JavaScript and a database. He picked PHP because it was the language he already knew from making a blog.
- He gets criticized for the stack and doesn't care: "it doesn't matter what you use, but as long as you use something that's really fast."
- Speed of the iteration loop is the point. He can add a button and deploy in about 20 seconds. Developer friends on heavier stacks (Kubernetes etc.) sometimes need an hour or days per feature.
- He ties this to lean startup: customer feedback has to loop fast.
- Fast shipping makes customers happy because they see their own request live and feel they "influenced this product."
- He builds features from talking to customers about what they want.

chunks.heading: Build for yourself, spot a "discongruence," and surf waves
chunks.text:
- He describes himself as "user zero." He builds what he needs.
- His idea trigger is a gap between what he sees and what society says. Most people assume something is wrong with them. He assumes society may be wrong and makes a small site to test it.
- Example: he tweeted about inflation about two years earlier, people dismissed it, so he built inflationchart.com to show higher real inflation numbers.
- Travel feeds product ideas indirectly. Different places and different shop products inspire him.
- The origin was not a master plan:
  - He started blogging about nomading in 2013 for his mom.
  - Posts about bootstrapping as a nomad in Asia took off on Hacker News.
  - Twitter followers grew organically from there.
  - His inspiration was Patrick McKenzie (patio11), an indie developer who shared revenue from small projects.
- He positioned against the "shady" online business scene he saw in Thailand and wanted reputable, mainstream remote work.
- On timing: he gave a talk in 2015 predicting 1 billion remote workers by 2030 and was ridiculed. COVID changed that.
- Pieter says he had no idea it was coming, and for years the chart "doesn't really go anywhere."
- His lesson: "You cannot control the market at all... Just surf waves." Pivoting is steering the surfboard.
- Movements start with freaks, then developers, then the mainstream, as with crypto and electronic music.

chunks.heading: Revenue as an asset, small starts, and why he doesn't sell
chunks.text:
- He tweeted that an app doing 20,000 a month is "probably already a millionaire." It implies about a 1M asset at a 4-5x multiple.
- He thinks 20K a month is approachable with high automation, high margins, and part-time contractors instead of a big team.
- Advice for small ideas: one feature done really well solves one problem, brings the first customers and cash flow, then you add a second feature and scale toward a real product toolkit.
- Why you rarely see multi-million bootstrapped founders: they raise VC once past 1M and go for a billion-dollar outcome. He chose not to.
- Why he hasn't sold:
  - Bootstrapped businesses usually fetch 3-5x, "too low for me."
  - He said 10x is where it gets interesting.
  - Most acquisition processes bounced off.
  - The sites run themselves, so he can just wait.
  - Nomad List is his "baby" and he expects buyers to ruin it. Remote OK is less personal because it's "just a job board."
- He used to be obsessed with selling because of startup movies, until his own cash flow made it matter less.
- He publishes /open pages with live stats, P&L and an estimated valuation based on a multiple of profit.

chunks.heading: Pricing and automated high-ticket sales on Remote OK
chunks.text:
- Job post prices range from about 100 to 1,000 dollars, with dynamic pricing. He changes job post pricing based on how many people post jobs on the site.
- He sells job post bundles via Stripe with no sales calls. Customers use a slider on remoteok.com/buy-bundle to build their own bundle and get a discount.
- Bundles are roughly 30% of revenue. Examples:
  - 25 jobs for 22,000 dollars.
  - Typical large purchases of about 40-50K.
  - The biggest ever was around 49-50K.
- Companies pay with company cards. The bundle idea came from companies asking if they could buy job posts in advance.
- The sales page is packed with text and emojis. He keeps adding content daily and says it "looks like a circus" but works.
- Hidden complexity: invoices for every little thing, edge cases, special features and dynamic pricing. This is why clones that copy the look don't take off.
- Self-serve customers (credit card on Stripe, no forms or NDAs) are, in his experience, more modern, pay more, and are easier to support. Customers who ask many email questions and want W-8 forms convert less and pay less.
- Sales team debate: the hosts argued sales teams create demand. Pieter conceded it might work but said he hasn't found good salespeople, fears managing them, and fears outbound spam damaging his reputation. He's optimizing for freedom and happiness rather than max growth.

chunks.heading: Radical transparency as a recurring marketing engine
chunks.text:
- Pieter publishes revenue and stats openly (revenue meter in his Twitter bio, /open pages).
- He says this "recurring marketing machine" is a big reason his businesses and Twitter audience grew: "I cannot deny that."
- His motivation is radical honesty and countering founders who only share the good news. He wants to show the ups and downs of a small indie company.
- He admits it's now part of his identity and hard to stop.
- The hosts' critiques (Buffer-style transparency gets harder at scale, and privacy concerns) were their views, though Pieter agreed it's hard to stop.
- Content format thoughts: he is wary of the weekly-content treadmill and burnout. He is considering short talking-head videos, as Derek Sivers does.
- He closed his DMs because most are low-quality asks from people who don't invest time, and he explained his routine in a blog post instead.

chunks.heading: Product opportunities Pieter sees in slow nomad and remote worker markets
chunks.text:
- Digital nomad is "a horrible word." His data says people travel slowly. The average stay is about seven months, and many have partners, kids and families.
- He says "slowmads" are the real market and are underserved. Moving weekly doesn't work for them.
- Opportunity ideas he gave:
  - Serviced apartment hotels for long stays, aimed at high-earning remote workers (100-200K). He spends about 2-3.5K a month on them and says they solve cleaning, breakage and quality variance versus Airbnb.
  - Furniture rental with a configurable "click and arrive, already set up" experience.
  - Homeschooling and education for remote families.
  - Pet-friendly travel and services, since tech workers have pets and often no kids.
- He prefers being a customer rather than owning real estate. He's a software guy.
- He sees remote work as still niche and growing as physical jobs get automated.

chunks.heading: Lifestyle, spending, and constraints
chunks.text:
- Pieter spends about 4-5K a month and invests the rest after tax, mostly in ETFs (Vanguard, S&P 500, some Asia exposure) plus Bitcoin and Ethereum.
- He benchmarked and found his S&P 500 ETF beat his own stock picks over two years. He sold roughly 70-80% of his individual stocks.
- He avoids lifestyle inflation deliberately, citing hedonic adaptation research and "golden handcuffs" he saw in corporate friends.
- Where he spends: food (organic, grass-fed) and experiences, and business class only on rare long-haul flights.
- He argues constraints help creativity and focus. He owns little: a backpack, a small suitcase, clothes, iPhone, MacBook Pro, backup phones for 2FA, and two Stadia controllers.
- He now mostly stays in one place (Portugal) with nomad friends nearby. His routine is coffee, coding a little with a friend, gym, sauna and swimming. He says he doesn't get bored as long as he ships a bit on his sites.
- He admires Derek Sivers (CD Baby founder, who sold it for 30 million dollars) as a model of a simple, philosophical life.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Levels shares the repeatable loop he found after launching many bootstrapped projects: solve your own problem, build fast alone, launch on Product Hunt/Hacker News/Reddit, grow organically, charge early, automate with scripts, then exit or move on. He stresses shipping small, validating with money, and avoiding paid or bot growth.

chunks.heading: Pieter's origin story and the 12 startups in 12 months project
chunks.text:
- Pieter graduated in business in the Netherlands. He ran a YouTube channel for electronic music making about $2,000-$3,000 a month, then sold his stuff and traveled Asia with a laptop.
- The YouTube income fell from roughly $3,000 to $900, then $700, then $500 while he traveled. He returned to his parents' house with anxiety, depression and panic attacks.
- His fix was to "do 12 projects in 12 months", one month each, as a way to keep busy and build something.
- Early projects: a playlist app for music shared by email (no revenue), and animated GIF flip books via a Malaysian printer (margin only 2-3%, probably losing money after tax).
- The first that made money was a goal-commitment app. You set a goal and deadline (e.g. quit smoking by 1 January), add a prize and a credit card via Stripe, and a friend confirms by email. If the friend says no, the card is charged $50-$100 and the money goes to him. It took him from about $200 a month to about $700 a month.
- The press picked up the "12 startups in 12 months" project (The Next Web, Tech in Asia). Thousands of people emailed him and followed him on Twitter. He says he "cracked this little marketing thing accidentally".
- He did only about 7 of the 12. Nomad List took off and he chose to grow it rather than keep launching new projects. It took "hardcore effort" and constant feature work.

chunks.heading: The shotgun approach and what stuck
chunks.text:
- Pieter's philosophy: "shotgun", shoot lots of projects and see which one sticks.
- **Nomad List** began as a public spreadsheet of cities (internet speed, temperature around 26°C, cost of living). He accidentally left it editable, so people added data and it went viral, reaching about 75 cities. He turned it into a website and launched on Hacker News, where it hit number one. Now about 1,250 cities and 250,000 crowdsourced data points, making $15,000-$25,000 a month in membership fees.
- **Remote OK** is a remote job site, since December the number-one remote job site in the world with almost a million monthly visits, making about $10,000 a month.
- **Hoodmaps** is a crowdsourced map tagging neighborhoods (hipster, rich, tourist).
- The recurring loop he describes: idea, build, launch, grow, monetize, automate, exit, repeat.
- Only one product in the early batch stuck, and he treats that as normal.

chunks.heading: Finding ideas and validating them
chunks.text:
- Solve your own problems. "You are the expert at your own problems", which is a competitive advantage (a gardener knows gardeners' problems). Nomad List came from wanting to know which cities to go to; Hoodmaps from being lost in tourist centers.
- Because people are homogeneous, they get the same ideas. To be more original, do unusual things (skydiving, long solo jungle treks, fringe subcultures). Taboo areas have less competition.
- Start small: fix a small niche problem, make money, then grow the niche. Elon Musk started with PayPal, not a space company. Nomad List is now expanding into the whole travel market, which he estimates is 10-100x bigger.
- A $100 product needs only 10,000 customers to make $1 million.
- Keep a concepts list of every idea. The ones that keep coming back are worth building; some remote work ideas came months before he built them.
- Competitors: an existing app does not mean there's no market. If nothing exists, usually there is no market. Existing apps are often broken, ugly and low-usage, so you can make a better one. He is "a little bit arrogant and naive" and jumps straight in; it works about one in ten times. Think from first principles about the problem you want to solve.
- Do it yourself, no co-founder. Groupthink is dangerous; people hype each other's ideas. Working alone ships faster.
- Share your ideas. "Nobody's gonna steal your idea, it's all about execution." Sharing lets you talk to potential customers before you build.

chunks.heading: Learning to build and keeping the prototype short
chunks.text:
- Don't do coding bootcamps (he calls them "a little bit of a scam"). Google "how to make a website". The core skill is learning how to learn and figure things out yourself.
- He started with spreadsheets and basic WordPress themes and learned just in time: when a problem appeared, he googled it. "The only other option of not learning it was my entire startup failing."
- He uses PHP and vanilla JavaScript and finds JS frameworks needlessly difficult. Even professional developers spend half their time googling and copy-pasting from Stack Overflow.
- No-code options for non-coders: Typeform (forms that accept Stripe payments) and a no-code site builder built by his friend AJ.
- Prototype in a maximum of one month. Months of polishing with no customers doesn't work; you need to validate by launching.
- He thinks coding is essential: "if you're not coding you're gonna be unemployed".

chunks.heading: Launching: Product Hunt, Hacker News, Reddit and niche communities
chunks.text:
- Launching is the validation step. Do Product Hunt, Reddit and Hacker News on the same day to concentrate traffic and create a compounding effect, plus tweet and share on Facebook.
- **Product Hunt**: about 10,000 visits, roughly 10% convert or less. Make the listing look good, add an animated GIF, write a very simple slogan (ask friends). It runs on San Francisco time, so submit just after midnight SF time to rank high that day. Reply to comments, fix bugs immediately, be human, not marketing.
- **Hacker News**: its comments can "destroy your whole startup". Use a "Show HN", be frank, honest and personal. No voting rings or bots.
- **Reddit**: about 100x bigger than Product Hunt and Hacker News, and the mainstream launch platform. Post in niche subreddits (e.g. r/horses for a horse management app), friendly and asking for feedback. Front-page traffic can reach 400,000 to half a million visits. He hit the front page twice (including Hoodmaps).
- Make the site static HTML rather than PHP or JS and load test it, since servers die at page two or three of the front page.
- Niche forums and websites for your audience may convert highest because they're so relevant.
- For non-web or offline products, go where customers are. Patrick McKenzie (patio11) sold his appointment reminder SMS app by walking into barber shops and hair salons.
- After launch, traffic spikes then drops, which is normal. If everyone is gone within a week, it may not be validated.
- To judge whether to continue, he keeps a Google bookmark of his product name in quotation marks filtered to the past 24 hours or week to see press mentions. Give a product a few weeks, not months: "just do new stuff".
- Keep relaunching: launch features and major versions to the press every few months to stay in people's minds.

chunks.heading: Organic growth, feedback loops and building in public
chunks.text:
- He hates "non-organic" growth: Instagram bots, Twitter follow/unfollow bots, bought email lists and ads. Paid traffic fades when you stop paying, and it hides whether the product is any good.
- Organic traffic is the "ultimate test" of product quality. If you don't get it, the product isn't good enough.
- Every site has a feedback box ("be nice"). He adds features weekly (e.g. moved a search box because someone said it looked ugly). Users become ambassadors through co-creation. Intercom works but is paid.
- Capture emails to re-engage users after launch spikes, e.g. daily job alerts and a newsletter for Remote OK. Use sparingly.
- Build in public. He live-streamed building Hoodmaps (about 100 viewers made him code faster) and cites Drew Wilson doing it. It brings attention and press, and few others do it.
- Press and Twitter: he warns to ignore haters and not engage.

chunks.heading: Monetization, pricing and business models
chunks.text:
- Charge early: aim for the first dollar within about two months, ideally on launch day. Without revenue the idea isn't validated.
- Ignore the "this should be free" complainers, especially on Reddit. You compete with free alternatives by being premium.
- Validate with fake doors:
  - Buffer put up a landing page with plans and a pricing button that collected emails, validating demand before building.
  - Pieter built a fake Stripe payment box for a feature he hadn't built. It saved no card data and said it was a test, collecting emails of those who paid. Then he built the feature and those people paid. "Put buy buttons on everything."
- Charge limits from the start; it's harder to limit free features later. He regrets giving too much of Nomad List away free and says he could have charged $10 for all features.
- Side-product models: the main product can be free while something adjacent earns.
  - Nomad List data is free; about 7,000 people pay for membership (the social network for travelers).
  - Dribbble is free for designers, but employers pay $299 for 30 days to post jobs.
  - Sponsorships: Matt Mullenweg's Automattic (WordPress) sponsored Nomad List with a banner and was hiring, paying a few thousand dollars a month. It's hard to get by outbound emailing.
  - Patreon/supporter models: a Japan YouTuber makes $3,000 a month from 800 supporters; Overcast has a patron tier at around $12.
- Nomad List membership: he started charging because of spammers in the chat (people selling courses). He put $5 behind a Typeform, then raised it to $25, $50, then $100, and people kept paying. Spam nearly disappeared. Now about $1 a day or $99 a year, and you can browse read-only but need to pay to have a profile and interact.
- Prefer recurring revenue. With 25% yearly sales growth, a one-time $75 payment gives $75,000 in year one and about $183,000 by year five, versus almost $2 million a year with subscriptions.

chunks.heading: Automation, solo operations and exits
chunks.text:
- Pieter gets bored of products after 1-2 years, so he automates. His server runs 180-700 robots (cron jobs and parallel processes) at once, e.g. fetching weather for Nomad List, collecting remote job posts, and processing refunds.
- He prefers scripts to hiring because humans are hard to fire and get sick. The one human role: one full-time person on standby to monitor servers and alerts, so you aren't woken at 4 a.m.
- Software scales: 40 visitors or 4,000 on Reddit with no change and no hiring. He tried a social media manager (Buffer posts) but sees little future in content work.
- Work comes in cycles of intense sprints, then little work. Products get dusty as trends change.
- Legal: one company holding everything as projects, because a Dutch BV/LLC would cost at least about $5,000 a year in bookkeeping.
- Exit: a business with $100,000 a year and 25% growth could sell for about $500,000, or around $1 million with higher growth. He'd want a 4-5x revenue multiple and has declined offers because he wasn't happy with the price. He notes the emotional attachment to a "baby" product.
- Mistakes he names: trusting TechCrunch-style advice (raise millions, hire a team, get an office) instead of his intuition, and engaging with haters. He advises trusting your own intuition and being nicer.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Levels explains why indie hacking is now crowded and competes with funded companies, and how that plays out in AI startups where there is no moat, thin margins and supplier risk. He shares how he validates ideas manually with a landing page and payment link, and why he favors simple, old tech and going where the herd isn't.

chunks.heading: Why Pieter says "indie hacking is dead"
chunks.text:
- His point: indie hacking started around 2014-2016 (with Product Hunt) and became mainstream. Like "remote hacking" would have died once Covid made remote work normal, it's no longer "hacking", just normal business.
- Big tech and VC-funded AI startups now follow him and other indie makers on Twitter. If he launches a feature, they ask their developers to build the same one.
- He sees indie hackers sleeping in a $600/month pod hostel in San Francisco to ship AI startups, which he takes as proof it's mainstream.
- Consequence: more competitive, more saturated, harder. He competes with companies that raised $500 million.
- Recession and burned-out VC-funded founders make lean, bootstrapped building a necessity. Several VC-funded friends say their next startup will "preferably" be indie.
- Advice for beginners: "you should always do the opposite everybody else is doing." Now that indie hacking is mainstream, go where nobody is going and "look for the part of the grass where nobody is".

chunks.heading: Moats, margins and platform dependency in AI startups
chunks.text:
- Moat is the big problem for AI startups, including VC-funded ones he talks to. Retention (churn) is very high and defensibility is low.
- Everyone uses the same models (GPT-4, Llama, Stable Diffusion), so it isn't proprietary tech. The stuff built around the models is proprietary, but a smart competitor can copy it in about three months, a slower one in six months to a year.
- Competition pushes prices down, which is good for customers but pushes profit margins toward zero. GPU costs keep his AI margins low, and Nvidia can't produce enough chips.
- Supplier risk example: his fine-tuning provider charged $3 per training. After seeing his tweets about revenue, it raised the price to $20 per training while he sold for about $25-30. For a month they captured the money and he couldn't switch. Lesson: when you look successful, suppliers raise prices.
- He moved to Replicate, which he says is helpful and only decreases prices.
- Mitigation: abstract providers so you can swap, and note that platform dependency is lower now because there are many API providers.
- Running your own GPU servers is a level up, but needs Python skills he doesn't have, so he hired an AI developer.
- Stress: AI moves weekly, so you must implement new breakthroughs fast. He lifts (deadlift, squats, overhead press) to manage anxiety.

chunks.heading: Validate manually before writing code (Avatar AI)
chunks.text:
- Origin: he built interior AI, then tried fine-tuning on his own photos, tweeted the results, and it went viral. The next day he built Avatar AI.
- First version had no code: an index HTML page with example avatars and inputs, a Stripe payment link, and a Typeform after payment that collected photo uploads.
- He fulfilled about 100-200 orders manually: download photos, upload to the fine-tuning platform, download results. He worked all night, then started automating on day two. It took about a week to be fully automatic.
- Price was about $30 per order, which he describes as roughly $3,000-6,000 for a night's work.
- Result: about $400,000 (maybe half a million) in a month or two. Big VC-funded companies cloned it within a month and got much bigger (he cites about $40 million).
- Principle: "I'm not going to build anything until there's customers." This comes from spending about a year on a YouTube analytics startup around 2013-14 that nobody paid for.
- Rule of thumb: if automating takes longer than doing the thing by hand, just do it yourself until volume forces automation (he references the XKCD chart).

chunks.heading: Keep the tech stack simple and ship fast
chunks.text:
