- His stack is PHP, jQuery and SQLite. He says the "bad code" meme is exaggerated for viral effect. The code is structured, commented, in multiple files, on GitHub, with workers and a clear folder structure.
- He cites the Lindy effect (Taleb): old technology like PHP is proven because it has lasted. New tech needs more distrust.
- He argues web agencies and framework companies (he names Vercel's evangelists) push new tech as a sales and growth cycle, making developers think they need it.
- For entrepreneurs the priority is getting customers who pay, not elegant or over-engineered code.
- On speed: "I'm not a good developer but I'm really fast." He repeats himself rather than abstracting early; if code repeats ten times, then write a function.
- Landing pages: beautiful gradients and fancy design are "a red flag" before validation. Google and Facebook started very ugly. Behind 400 no-upvote Product Hunt launches are developers who spent six months on a perfect product.

chunks.heading: Learning his limits: hiring, SEO and TikTok
chunks.text:
- Until this year he did almost everything himself except customer support and chat moderators, plus a server person. He now says he hit complete limits (Python, GPUs, marketing).
- He hired an AI developer for the models, and a person for TikTok marketing.
- Danny Postma (Headshot Pro) is a peer: they swap tech tips every few weeks. Danny is a strong SEO guy who builds startups from keyword research (found that LinkedIn headshots drove most searches). Danny beating him in revenue pushed Pieter to learn SEO: look at what keywords people search and make sub pages.
- One TikTok influencer posting about photoai.com took his MRR from about 12K to 40-50K, and it stayed. Influencers had a much bigger effect than press, which he says does almost nothing (nobody clicks the logos).

chunks.heading: Distribution advice in 2023 and Twitter dynamics
chunks.text:
- If starting today he probably wouldn't use Twitter/X. He'd go to TikTok, see what people want, and document the journey ("I'm starting out, I want to make a startup and pay my rent, every day I'll make a video").
- Find startup ideas in subreddits ("every category becomes a startup", like the Craigslist meme); the Reddit of the day is TikTok.
- Catch technology waves and add a front end: new tech is hard to use, so making it easy gives a first mover advantage. Nomad List did the same by collecting scattered travel blog info. When ChatGPT and Stable Diffusion launched he scrambled to build many things and see what stuck, because waiting six months would be too late.
- Twitter's algorithm now tests tweets early (watch time) and pumps winners; many tweets get almost nothing despite 300K followers. Product updates get fewer views. Long posts get more because of dwell time, so he writes blog posts there.
- Packageable first sentences help: people who answer in one clear sentence and then go long form get clipped and get more views.
- He tweets honestly, with "strong opinions weakly held", and says most of his friends came from Twitter. He avoids "clickbait" listicles.

chunks.heading: Long-term businesses vs hype, and selling
chunks.text:
- Nomad List: about nine years old, usually $40-60K per month with low costs. He expected it to fade like his electronic music YouTube channel did. He is working on a 3D globe and would return to improve it once AI backlog is done.
- Contrast: AI is stressful and gimmicky (Avatar AI "felt so kitschy"), while Photo AI is meant as a long-term photo studio where people can have unlimited AI photos without a camera.
- Exit plan: grow Photo AI and Interior AI to about $100K MRR, cut costs, then sell via a broker. Valuations he got: AI startups can get about 5-8x profit versus 2-3x for typical startups, but multiples are based on profit, so he must cut GPU costs.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Levels explains why he picked indie hacking over VC funding: validate first, avoid the go-big-or-bust trap, and keep small projects alive for years. He also covers replacing hires with GPT, building an audience by posting constantly, and relying on ChatGPT referrals because he dislikes SEO.

chunks.heading: Why Pieter prefers the indie hacker path over VC
chunks.text:
- He says the main thing he hates about VC is seeing companies with no users raise $50M or $100M on hype, with no traction, and then disappear.
- He recommends validating first and building a real business before scaling, e.g. getting to 50K or 100K a month.
- Raising money locks in a "go big or bust" expectation. As a founder you can't easily stay in between: you can't make $10M a year, you "kind of need to make $100 million a year" and become a unicorn.
- He notes the odds of becoming a unicorn are "a few percentage maybe", and people spend five to seven years of their 20s on it.
- The indie alternative: a $10M a year company where you keep ownership. He calls this liberating.
- He says that in 2013-14 there was no indie hacking or bootstrapping scene. The norm was raise money, grow fast, hire a lot of people, get a big office.
- Despite being financially independent and getting VC DMs, he hasn't raised. He says playing with other people's money "sounds fun" but he isn't convinced yet.
- He has started investing as an angel (Cursor is one example) but says he feels like a "faker".

chunks.heading: Scale, portfolio and what the business looks like
chunks.text:
- His businesses make more than $3 million a year in revenue, run solo.
- Figures cited in the interview: Nomad List reached $700K ARR, Remote OK about $3.4-4M in revenue, Photo AI $600K ARR.
- He has launched about 70 projects, possibly more, and loses track.
- He tries to keep most of them running because he likes keeping "internet history" alive.
- Go Fucking Do It (gofuckingdoit.com) is a commitment product: you set a goal and deadline, name a friend as referee, and enter a card via Stripe. The card is not charged up front. On the deadline the friend is emailed, and if they say you failed, you are charged and he keeps the money.
- That product still earns about $50 a month. He hasn't changed the PHP code in 10 years.
- He started making money in 2014, when Stripe arrived in Holland.
- Earlier, he monetised music on YouTube as one of the first monetised channels, making $1,000 to $8,000 a month while still at university.

chunks.heading: Make things to solve your own problems
chunks.text:
- His origin story: for a decade he worked on his laptop, traveling and making small creative projects to solve his own problems.
- Most of the time nobody else needed them. "A few times it worked."
- He learned from Patrick McKenzie's Appointment Reminder, which made $60,000 a year, and from Yongfook (Singapore, nomad, a well-built SaaS).
- What inspired him was seeing "honest cool clean businesses" that were not VC-funded.
- He argues that profit comes from many shots at small projects rather than one big bet.

chunks.heading: Audience, brand and distribution
chunks.text:
- A host noted he sold $50,000 of pre-orders for his book before writing it.
- He attributes this partly to his brand and partly to work: he tweeted about 125,000 times over 10 years, roughly 40 tweets a day.
- He says ChatGPT referrals have grown fast. Google traffic was about 100 against ChatGPT at about 4, i.e. 4%. A month before the interview it was 20%, a 5x jump, and he saw the same story on other sites.
- He says this helps because he hates SEO and is a solo person who just wants to "make a cool product and a cool website with a nice title".

chunks.heading: Automate instead of hiring
chunks.text:
- He dislikes hiring because he doesn't like managing people and prefers creating things.
- Automation is what lets one person run multiple projects.
- Example: the Nomad List community chat (about 40,000 people) was draining to moderate by hand, with constant drama and accusations of bias.
- He now writes down the chat rules and has the GPT API moderate. It doesn't ban people; it mutes them for ten minutes or a day, like debate moderators muting mics.
- He says the AI is neutral, which a human moderator can't be.
- His rule of thumb: either hire people or use the GPT API, and he picks the API.

chunks.heading: Money, investing and product ideas
chunks.text:
- He recommends index funds (S&P 500, MSCI World) and not selling in drawdowns.
- He warns against home-country bias, citing his parents holding Royal Dutch Shell and Dutch stocks instead of S&P 500.
- He says to put founder income into the market rather than spend it all, since startup earning time is limited.
- He suggested a European-focused index investing product as a business idea, since good products for Europeans are lacking. The host's counterpoint was that resale margins are thin at Vanguard-like fees (0.07%).
- Personal finance isn't taught in school and cash "disappears the moment you have it."

chunks.heading: Stripe feedback and working with payments
chunks.text:
- He says the Stripe API got more complicated after COVID and felt "run by engineers, not by people who actually use Stripe".
- His example: a change to the API stopped creating a customer so everyone became a guest, a default he found illogical.
- He thinks it has improved and that "sanity has returned".
- He wants Stripe to keep its original simplicity: one line of Stripe.js gave you a payment button.
- His own usage: he goes to Stripe to see how much money he made, then goes back to coffee and code. He doesn't have time for advanced features like workflows.
- He says to avoid becoming corporate as a company grows, and to expose users slowly to what's possible.

chunks.heading: Europe and EU accelerationism
chunks.text:
- He started an "EU accelerationism" push, inspired by effective accelerationism in the US, with a crowdsourced bug board where tens of thousands submitted and upvoted ideas to fix Europe.
- His top idea: remove the regulatory burden for new businesses, and kill cookie banners.
- He argues Europe needs politics that is both pro-business and pro-federal Europe, which doesn't currently exist.
- His view: "Getting rich is simply a representation of your added value to the world economy in most cases." He says Europeans should drop the idea that business and getting rich is bad.
- He says it's good it's going badly now: "Never waste a crisis."

chunks.heading: Digital nomad lifestyle
chunks.text:
- He has lived in more than 40 countries and 150 cities.
- He recommends anyone try it regardless of age. His first experience was a university exchange in Korea around 2010.
- He says it is safer than people think. In 10 years nothing happened to him; the only burglary was in his hometown.
- He admits it can be very lonely, and that you lose contact with your home culture and become "untethered", which takes years to rebuild.
- He advises staying flexible: "You need to be neuroflex."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Pieter Levels walks through his 12 startups in 12 months experiment and how Nomad List grew without funding, events or paid marketing. He lays out five stages (idea, build, launch, grow, monetize) and argues for solo building, repeated launches, organic growth and charging from day one.

chunks.heading: Pieter's case against startup scenes, conferences and mentors
chunks.text:
- Pieter argues most startup scenes outside Silicon Valley are "all about events" and conferences, with little actually being made. He singled out the Dutch government-backed startup ecosystem organizations as spending millions on events.
- He says networking coffee meetings mostly produce "investors" who turn out to be bullshitters.
- His rule: "just make stuff and then get it over with." Creativity is sitting alone in front of the laptop and doing it, not listening to someone at a conference.
- He thinks the academic habit of needing mentors and teachers is a trap for founders. You learn from doing, and "real reality is the best school."
- His TL;DR: be original, do cool things, don't take courses, learn the code yourself, learn the basics, and stop going to conferences and network events because you won't learn anything.
- He says ads don't work well anymore because people use ad blockers and want real things. The product itself has to become the marketing, like a great beer you come back for and tell friends about.

chunks.heading: How the 12 startups in 12 months experiment led to Nomad List
chunks.text:
- Pieter spent about a year building a YouTube analytics dashboard (database and API for managing multiple channels). Vice and other big media companies used it, then stopped. It made zero dollars.
- He then committed to launching one project every month and blogged it as "I'm launching 12 startups in 12 months." He finished roughly seven or eight, because Nomad List took over.
- Projects included:
  - Play My Inbox: scraped Gmail for YouTube music links into a playlist.
  - Giftbook: animated GIFs turned into flip books, sold roughly 500.
  - Goal-setting app with a charged credit card if you fail: went viral, made a lot of money, but wasn't a sustainable business.
  - Remote job board: filtered remote listings from other boards.
- Nomad List began as a Google spreadsheet of cities (cost, internet speed, climate) that he shared on Twitter. Thousands of people edited it, and he turned it into a website.
- It hit number one on Hacker News (600 points), number one on Product Hunt, and the front page of Reddit, then triggered press interviews.
- Later monetization: a paid social network for about $20-30 a month with almost 10,000 members, and a database of about 1,000 cities and 100,000 data points. Revenue went from about $5,000 a month to about $40,000 a month, "almost half a million a year."
- He built it alone from a laptop, owns 100%, had hardly any costs, no funding, and no paid marketing.
- His five stages: idea, build, launch, grow, monetize.

chunks.heading: Finding ideas: solve your own problems, get original, start small
chunks.text:
- Build for problems you personally have. You are the best customer, and if a thousand others pay $10 a month, that's $10,000 a month.
- Everyone has the same ideas (friend finders, photo apps, food delivery), so you must become a more original person.
- Ways he lists to become original:
  - Travel, which exposes you to new cultures and problems.
  - Work lots of different jobs, such as a factory or coffee shop, to see problems on the work floor.
  - Spend time in fringe subcultures.
  - Be early on fringe topics. Nomad work was very niche in 2014. He concedes it's a gamble but "better than being the same."
- His own ideas came from travel. The flip book idea came from seeing a shop in Hong Kong. He says sitting at home with the coffee machine produces no ideas.
- Start small with a hook rather than a "spaceship company." Example: instead of a generic travel tours app, a group travel app for women, which gives a story to pitch to press. You can expand later.
- Nomad List started as a social network for digital nomads and is expanding to travelers.

chunks.heading: Building: do it yourself, keep it simple, automate, work alone
chunks.text:
- Don't outsource development. Changing a button color through a remote team takes meetings and days, while doing it yourself takes five seconds. He wants a fast feedback loop.
- Learn just the basics, just in time. He compares it to learning to ride a bicycle, not racing like Lance Armstrong. Skip big frameworks like Meteor and Angular, which he says are a year-long rabbit hole and make some startups take six months to get a landing page online.
- Use the tools you know. Suggested MVP tools:
  - Public spreadsheets (his own started as one).
  - Typeform, which can even take payments.
  - Squarespace with e-commerce.
  - WordPress or basic HTML and PHP.
- Automate from day one. His sites run cron jobs, "robots on my server," that fetch weather or find co-working spaces and add them to the site, freeing him to build features and validate ideas.
- Put a buy button in the MVP, even a fake one. If someone enters card details, show a pop-up saying "we're not live yet, we haven't saved your card, we'll email you when we're done." That validates demand. He cites a startup that began with a "plans and pricing" button and an email box.
- Work alone. Competing VC-funded teams of 20 in Silicon Valley take months to add a feature. His "meeting" is thinking in bed what to add tomorrow, then adding it. Hire contractors later if needed.

chunks.heading: Launch tactics: prepare it, press, Product Hunt, Hacker News, Reddit
chunks.text:
- Launch is "the most important stage." If you mess it up, product quality won't matter.
- An MVP is ready when the bugs are gone and basic functionality works. He criticizes launching a landing page with only an email box, because nothing has been built.
- Preparation checklist:
  - Add analytics (he admits he forgets and later finds zero data).
  - Collect emails, because launch day brings 10,000-20,000 visitors who mostly won't return.
  - Add a feedback form (he used Olark) so bugs reach him immediately.
- Press: find journalists relevant to your niche, not just TechCrunch. Make it a personal story, and keep it to one or two sentences, three at most. Send to 100 journalists and "maybe five will write about you."
- Product Hunt: email your existing list, tell them it's live, and don't ask them to vote. Upvotes can follow naturally.
- Hacker News: you need a few people to upvote early in the first hour, then the rest push it up. If it doesn't catch, it fails.
- Reddit: pick a subreddit relevant to the product that is also on the front page. Don't write a boastful title like "best app ever." Say plainly what you built and that it might be relevant.
- For niches, go to specialist forums (his example: a motorcycle forum), write a humble post, and keep interacting. Build requested features quickly, even on launch day, to get users engaged.
- After launch, check analytics (his example: 2,000 visitors, 6,000 euros). Traffic always drops afterward, which is normal. If the idea didn't work, scrap it.

chunks.heading: Growth: skip growth hacking, relaunch often, spin off features, re-engage
chunks.text:
- He says "[ __ ] growth hackers" and calls the scene sleazy, full of former SEO spammers and addictive social patterns. He prefers organic growth where the product is the marketing.
- Don't pay for traffic early. Paid users hide whether the startup is validated, and when the money runs out the users leave.
- Launch repeatedly. Instead of one launch, ship a new feature every few months and send it to press and relevant communities. He shows traffic spikes in May, July and August, with drops between that require new launches.
- Spin off features as standalone side projects:
  - After Brexit he rapidly reskinned Nomad List into an "escape the Brexit" site and sent it to UK press, getting lots of coverage and traffic.
  - He spun the co-working spaces feature out as a separate site, Place to Work, submitted it to Product Hunt and Hacker News, and it now sends traffic back to Nomad List.
  - Pick features that can live on their own and take them out.
- Tell stories to press about new features, such as strategy or a bigger market, rather than "we added a feature."
- Build in public, like Buffer sharing revenue and every good or bad event.
- Make sharing easy. Generate dynamic preview images for every page (for example a San Francisco city page) so links get far more clicks on Facebook and Twitter.
- Re-engage old users with web push notifications and emails. When he launched Nomad List 2 he emailed users, asked them to reply directly, and got traffic and engagement.
- Keep shipping like Snapchat's weekly new filters. If nobody uses a new feature, scrap it and focus on what is monetizable.

chunks.heading: Monetization: charge early, recurring memberships, and other models
chunks.text:
- If you make zero dollars "you're doing a hobby and it's not a real startup." He says developers feel guilty charging, which is wrong given the weeks spent building.
- Free apps lose more money as they grow and when they explode. Paid apps make more money as they grow. So charge immediately and think about monetization at the start. He says his early Play My Inbox never earned because he didn't think about it.
- Business models he discusses:
  - Affiliate: poor. Hotel bookings on Nomad List gave about five bucks for five bookings.
  - Display ads: "dead."
  - Native text ads: work. Sell them yourself or via networks, or add a simple text link.
  - Sponsorships: Matt Mullenweg of WordPress/Automattic emailed to sponsor Nomad List on launch, giving about 2,000-4,000 dollars a month immediately and making him profitable. He suggests cold emailing companies to sponsor.
  - Paid membership: gate the chat group behind a "join a community" paywall. He made it recurring, about $30 a month, and says user count builds up so revenue "almost double[s] every year."
  - Patronage: a friend's YouTube channel about Japan has 835 patrons paying about 3,000 a month. Overcast dropped premium features and asks for optional payment.
- Put buy buttons on everything to validate demand.

chunks.heading: Build for future trends and when to ditch an idea
chunks.text:
- Be ahead of the curve. Trends he names:
  - Short-term relationships and less marriage.
  - Less home ownership, more renting and travel.
  - Changing family units and co-living.
  - Local food and robot farms.
  - An "existential crisis" from comfort, so entertainment or products that address it.
  - Basic income.
  - 3D, VR and AR, which he is currently learning (building an interactive Japan street in Unity).
- Ditch rule: if it isn't making money or getting traffic after a few months, scrap it. He criticizes people who spend years on something that will never work and call it determination.
- On boring work plus life: grinding four hours with headphones, then going salsa dancing, was a good combination of boring and amazing. He says living in a place for more than two weeks changes your identity, since it's shaped by your environment.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Growth Tribe panel with Pieter Levels, Marc Köhlbrugge and others on shipping early, engineered marketing and data. The transcript has no speaker labels, so only the clearest Levels-style statements are kept: visualizing the future as the source of products, trusting intuition over A/B testing, and press as a sustained traffic source. Attribution is low confidence.

chunks.heading: Shipping early and building for yourself
chunks.text:
- Pieter's advice to his younger self: "ship my products earlier, don't perfect them." He says to just ship.
- His own first project was a huge analytics dashboard that took 1.5 years of work, and nobody paid for it.
- Marc, a co-panelist, describes the opposite lesson. Pieter's takeaway is the same: ship things people actually want before putting in a year of effort.
- His current approach is to make sure someone will actually use a product before pouring time into it, rather than building maximum functionality without asking whether anyone needs it.
- He frames this as the Lean Startup approach.

chunks.heading: Small steps beat big visions
chunks.text:
- Pieter visualizes the future vividly (where he wants to be in ten years, how the house looks, how it feels). He says visions already exist in you and you "dig into yourself" to find them.
- He ties this to his nomad startups: he remembers being in the Philippines at night, picturing many people traveling and working, before building Nomad List-type products.
- He says you can pursue a big vision with small websites and small steps.
- He recommends a monthly float tank session (about 40 dollars in Amsterdam) as a way to get visions.

chunks.heading: Data, A/B testing and intuition
chunks.text:
- Pieter says he uses very little data for his products. He sees many people A/B testing and tracking events, but he doesn't really trust it.
- He prefers intuition: have a feeling for your product and how you would use it. "Humans are not numbers."
- He argues that optimizing mostly improves a local maximum; creativity and art make the big jumps, and art "never listens to the people that watch it."
- He cites Apple as a company that doesn't rely on focus groups, and Ford's "faster horses" idea as the reason not to over-rely on customer asks.
- He warns that over-optimized landing pages can produce customers who "hate" you: they got pulled to a green button, paid, and don't know what your site even is.
- His preferred stance is a modest approach: happy customers and a business built to enjoy life, "it's not all about sales."
- He personally tracks his own life with the Gyroscope app (connected to RescueTime and health data) for feedback loops like step counts.
- Other panelists argue for mixing hard and soft data; Pieter's position is intuition-first.

chunks.heading: Press as a sustained acquisition channel
chunks.text:
- Pieter says press is almost completely the reason he is invited to events like this one.
- It only works if the product backs it up: "if it sucks they're not going to care, but if it's a good product and the press is there, it's so important and it keeps giving traffic."
- Example: a TNW (The Next Web) article keeps sending traffic for years because people searching his product's name still find it, as a top-three search result.
- He calls press one of the biggest sustained sources of traffic.
- Keep launching new features and products to keep generating press.
- Retargeting didn't work for him: he spent around 2,000 dollars on Facebook retargeting and says it hardly worked, so he is distrustful of it.

chunks.heading: Spinning off small products as a gateway to bigger ones
chunks.text:
- Pieter says engineered marketing works like a "gateway drug": small products or features attract a new audience, then you upsell to the bigger product.
- Apple example: the iPod brought people in, then iTunes worked well, then they might buy a MacBook or iMac.
- Big companies can use it too: if you have an expensive or hard-to-sell product, start with easier-to-buy products, establish a relationship with the customer, and later upsell.
- Spin-offs help you reach new markets beyond your brand's current audience (e.g., reaching business travelers beyond digital nomads).
- Note: an in-room panelist claims he coined the "gateway drug" framing; Pieter's point is the tactic itself.

chunks.heading: Finding eyeballs and channels for a new product
chunks.text:
- His blunt first answer: build something really valuable and interesting.
- He lists places to launch: BetaList, Product Hunt, Twitter, Medium, Hacker News.
- He stresses the concrete question to ask is: where are your customers, and which channels, conferences, websites or agencies do they use?
- For a product aimed at laid-off or unemployed people, he suggests:
  - Go to where customers are and strike a deal with intermediaries (e.g., lawyers, HR departments, companies doing layoffs), possibly offering commission.
  - Study competitors using tools like SimilarWeb, Google, and their Facebook and LinkedIn pages.
  - Target on Facebook or LinkedIn, and consider job boards.
  - Use referrals, since one customer in a community usually brings more.
  - Consider a chat or coaching service format.
- He also suggests building a small tool that solves a customer's problem, connecting with them, getting first value, then onboarding them to the main product.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Four-hour AMA where Levels explains why scrappy, ugly products win, why he avoids VC and ads, and how he prices Nomad List and Remote OK. He covers error reporting via Telegram, lifetime pricing vs churn, motivation hacks, and building communities.

chunks.heading: Shipping crude products and ignoring "enterprise" standards
chunks.text:
- Pieter argues that dev culture pushes people to build things in a "proper" way (complex code, perfect design, big-company look), and that this keeps small indie devs down.
- His analogy is a bakery: if people like your bread, they will come to a crappy shack and pay in nickels. "You can get a cash register later."
- The first version of Google also looked bad, so every first version looks bad.
- He built Remote OK as a single PHP file for a long time. He tweets self-deprecating jokes about how bad his code is, and uses that as marketing to show that code quality is not what matters.
- His stack is vanilla PHP, vanilla JavaScript with jQuery, no frameworks, SQLite, and Sublime Text as the editor.
- He built the instant messaging feature for Nomad List in about three hours with plain AJAX, then improved it slowly.
- Enterprise and freelance work focus on engineering and checklists. Entrepreneurship focuses on the customer side: what to build, how to get market fit, and how to get paying users.
- "Planning is procrastination." Fear of failure makes people prepare more instead of launching. Everything is bad at first, so launch and redo it.
- He learned to code on the spot, just in time. Early Nomad List loaded in 32 seconds because it pulled data from Google Sheets into JSON. It now loads in about 600 milliseconds.
- He did not know SQL when he started.

chunks.heading: Artisanal advantage over big companies
chunks.text:
- Pieter argues that people like artisanal products and small-team websites, and that companies like a direct line to the maker.
- Remote OK customers choose it over big boards like Indeed because they can email him to ask for a feature, such as a dashboard of all their jobs. He says he'll build it next month, which corporates will not do.
- Corporate answers like "maybe in Q5" are what people dislike. Small teams can be fast and give white-glove service.
- Authenticity is what people are "desperate for". Not everyone has to like the product: "80% of people don't like me... the 20% that does, they really, really like me." Don't try to appeal to everybody.
- He notes that everything big started small (Whole Foods started as a hippie vegetable store). "If you wanna get big, you need to start small."
- Bigger companies later buy small brands to buy access to the market.
- He says artisanal founders often burn out after about 10 years and sell, and the product then becomes corporate.

chunks.heading: Pricing Nomad List: lifetime vs monthly, and the price ceiling
chunks.text:
- Pieter's pricing logic is to get the highest revenue possible. He tests prices on live traffic and watches sales within a day.
- Example: at $300 he expects about 50 signups, which is $15,000. At $75 with 800 signups a month, that is $60,000.
- If doubling the price makes sales drop by more than half, he knows he is past the sweet spot. He changes prices regularly to see if the market will now pay more, and puts them back if not.
- Monthly membership is $30. Nomads typically cancel around month 4 or 5, so the expected value is about $90 (about 3 months).
- He sets lifetime membership slightly above that expected value, at $99. The price was around $75 after Black Friday.
- Nomads are often temporary users or never actually become nomads, so recurring revenue is hard to retain. He prefers to take the money upfront as lifetime.
- There is a psychological barrier at $100 for B2C. Above $99 there is a big drop-off, and only inflation or more perceived value will move it.
- B2B has no such limit. Remote OK charges about $1,600 for a job post, which is cheap against a recruiter fee of about $3,000. Businesses pay with company cards.
- Nomad List has a light membership without social features, added during corona, which also sells well and can scale more easily than the community.
- Dating is built into Nomad List, like a Tinder for nomads, and is included in premium. He jokes that a "Nomad List Gold" tier might extract more.
- A Nomad List ad page with Stripe checkout took a $1,500 ad from Shopify, with no email back and forth.

chunks.heading: Community limits, scaling, and acquisitions
chunks.text:
- Pieter says Facebook ads for Nomad List did not work: "you get the wrong users" and "really shitty users".
- Nomad List's membership works because the community is tight-knit, and more random users hurt it. "It's hard to scale community." The site is a database plus a community.
- Over 800 people a month sign up as paid, up from about 200 for a long time.
- He pays a moderator to keep the community friendly.
- A job board like Remote OK is easier to scale with B2B ads.
- The community started as a Slack for nomads in 2014/2015. People spammed it, so he charged $1 and then $5, $25, $50 as a spam filter. That became the membership.
- He suggests asking your audience what they would pay for, rather than inventing a product.
- He is skeptical of venture capital and angel investing: "I think Angel investing is vanity." Raised money is not yours. It is "business money", and "over half goes straight to Facebook ads".
- His advice is to get revenue and own 100% of your company.
- Many startup people who are famous and active on Twitter are not rich, because they took stock that can't be sold. One company offered $8 million in its stock to acquire Nomad List, which he considered unsellable.
- Bootstrapped startups typically sell for about 2 to 4 times annual revenue on marketplaces like Empire Flippers (he mentions being offered about 3.7). VC-backed ones can be valued much higher.

chunks.heading: Automation, error reporting, and tooling
chunks.text:
- His productivity hack is to automate everything: invoicing, user deletion, moderation. MVPs are already automated, so full automation is not hard. Also build checks that the robots are doing the right work.
- Error reporting is a few lines: a PHP error calls a Telegram bot webhook via `file_get_contents` and posts into a chat group. JavaScript errors are caught by `window.onerror`, sent by AJAX to the server, and forwarded to Telegram. A part-time server helper (Daniel) is in the group and can jump in.
- He argues this is good enough for a team, and that fancy error tooling is too tedious.
- Tools he names: Sublime Text, Telegram (also for alerts), photop.com instead of Photoshop, and Gig/Now for deploying instead of FTP, which he used for six years.
- He uses wip.co (made by his friend Marc) for public "/done" to-do logging and accountability.
- He moved his blog to Ghost and emails about 9,000 subscribers when he posts. He dislikes email in general.
- He shares live revenue charts on his sites (slash open) as a transparency and marketing tactic.
- Block-then-unblock a Twitter follower, which he calls "Blunble", to make a hater unfollow. He wrote a script that does this for his mute list.

chunks.heading: Motivation, product cycles, and working style
chunks.text:
- Pieter says intrinsic motivation lasts about six months, after which "you hate everything you do". Money rolling in is what keeps him working on a site, and projects that don't earn tend to die.
- Options for project fatigue after years: hire people to take over (he is hiring a developer and a customer support person) or sell.
- He is hiring a generalist PHP/JavaScript/CSS dev. He pays well, about double or triple market rates, to give people freedom.
- He is stepping away from Nomad List and Remote OK because he needs distance to find new ideas.
- New ideas need novel experiences, so he deliberately does other things.
- He launched several smaller products in the last year, including a QR menu, an idea generator on GPT-3, and Rebase (relocation and immigration agency for remote workers, with immigration lawyers, like Stripe Atlas for relocation).
- Bug fixes and maintenance are short (5-10 minutes). New products need long deep sessions, sometimes at night.
- He sleeps from about 3-4 a.m. to 11 a.m.-noon without an alarm, and says forcing an early-bird schedule is bad. No fixed schedule, with walks and gym every second day with a friend as accountability.
- "Making new stuff is the most fun. Growing stuff's kinda boring."
- Small wins help: sticky notes on a laptop, or logging `/done`. "I don't care about the task itself. I care about the feeling of finishing a task."
- When depressed, he still shipped a small task, because "that system keeps me on the rails".

chunks.heading: Reinventing yourself and the personal-brand approach
chunks.text:
- Pieter got labeled the digital nomad guy and found it cringe, so he moved to "indie / solo entrepreneur" as his brand. You have to keep reinventing yourself.
- He started Nomad List because the nomad scene was full of fake "dream lifestyle" course sellers and he wanted real people. He was inspired by a Singaporean-British founder making SaaS and traveling.
- Organic growth is proof you're right, and lack of it is proof you're wrong. He says marketing that looks like marketing is bad marketing.
- He says it is a mistake to want 100 shallow viewers over 20 engaged ones, because the core can grow. He treats top of funnel vs bottom of funnel the same for any audience.
- Companies are not loyal to you, so don't treat a company like family. "Family" culture reduces your negotiating power. He says he pays people for work and doesn't pretend otherwise.
- He argues for profit sharing or shared ownership for employees.
- He says avoid news, which is built to make people angry. He prefers neutral outlets like Reuters and The Economist.
- Nomad List data: about 140,000 trips logged. He uses it to publish public trends pages (for example, fastest-growing remote work hubs) as quick PHP pages.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Levels explains how he picks markets by spotting fringe behavior that many people secretly want, why he ships many projects expecting most to fail, and why launches must fit each platform. He also covers starting with a side gig and living cheaply to extend runway, plus how Rebase (Portugal immigration) took off.

chunks.heading: Starting with 70 projects, and why most fail
chunks.text:
- Pieter says he has launched "over 70 products projects" and only three or four worked out, such as Nomad List and Remote OK.
- He puts the odds of any single startup working at about 3 to 4 percent, even when you do well.
- His advice: "you need to try like 20 30 times." One project worked on for a year will probably fail.
- A first product will probably fail and so will the second. The failure is a reality check that your product has to be better or cheaper to matter.
- He warns against founders who say "I'm gonna build a billion dollar company" and won't share the idea. They launch and "nobody cares."

chunks.heading: Finding ideas at the fringe of what people secretly want
chunks.text:
- Pieter's test for a market: be where many people are privately thinking the same thing but aren't yet saying or doing it.
- Nomad List came from watching 20 to 40 nomads already living in Chiang Mai. They were a "fringe" group of slightly weird people doing something new.
- Rebase (immigration as a service for moving to Portugal) came from his own move and from people repeatedly asking him how to do the same.
- He quotes the idea that what nerds do on the weekends, everybody else does in the week ten years later.
- He argues people self-censor ideas that feel too crazy. Being "radically honest" about what you think surfaces what others secretly think.
- Doing what everyone else is doing gives horrible results. You need to be on the edge of something new.
- He credits timing and topic over launch technique. The remote work and nomad topic had been hot since 2014. People point to his followers, but he says that wasn't true at the start.

chunks.heading: How Rebase started, step by step
chunks.text:
- Origin: he registered as a Portuguese resident himself after living in Ericeira during Covid, and had immigration lawyers and tax advisers check his setup.
- People kept asking to do the same. He first made a Typeform and referred his immigration advisors, getting some paying customers.
- In November he built a landing page and launched it on Twitter with a photo of his laptop on his bed: "POV: building an immigration as a service startup." It went viral and got 500 signups in a month.
- His naive approach: take slow, email-and-invoice-and-bank-wire processes and put them on Stripe with digital forms. He says you need a naive perception that this will work.
- Current scale as he states it: 400 to 500 applicants per month, and he says that rate would be about 10 percent of Portuguese immigration, roughly 50,000 to 60,000 people moving to Portugal a year.
- He says Rebase makes "two to three million a year" with almost no expenses, though he doesn't say whether that is revenue or profit.
- His pride is in helping Venezuelan families get out. He calls it "a PHP script in Excel" saving people.

chunks.heading: Launch platforms are different from each other
chunks.text:
- Pieter's biggest annoyance: people who write a tweet, then post the same thing to Instagram, TikTok and Reddit. Each platform behaves differently.
- Reddit is "completely anti-spam." The only way to use it is to be a beneficial community member, give value and ask for feedback, not announce "I launched my startup."
- Nobody cares that you launched a startup. Put yourself in the reader's shoes and ask whether you would click.
- He says people overestimate their own idea's specialness, and a real launch gives a reality check.

chunks.heading: Side gig first, savings and cheap living second
chunks.text:
- He recommends starting as a side gig. He cites his own path: YouTube music channels earned him $1,000 to $2,000 a month, sometimes $8,000, during university (2008 to 2010).
- That income was his base when he left in April 2014. His first real money from nomad projects came around August 2014, over a year later.
- Warns about "golden handcuffs": the higher your salary climbs, the harder it is to leave, because earning 5k or 10k alone takes years.
- Use freedom to live somewhere cheap. In Chiang Mai he paid about $200 a month for a hotel room and a dollar or so for a meal. A small town in your own country also works.
- Cheap living can multiply your runway (he says about 5x versus an Amsterdam rent of 1,500 or more).
- He says university is a good time to work on projects because you barely need to attend.
- Don't run out of money and have to go back. He doesn't recommend burning your ships on savings alone.

chunks.heading: Why entrepreneurship is closer to art than corporate business
chunks.text:
- He did a business bachelor's and an entrepreneurship master's, and says entrepreneurship is "way closer to creativity" than to corporate management, which he traces to 1950s US military management theory.
- Compares entrepreneurs to artists: you make things nobody likes for years, and it is emotionally exhausting because nothing you do works. The difference with a job is you don't get paid from day one.
- He calls it "one of the hardest things to do in life," a thing that takes sacrifice, and says the barrier to entry is why not everyone succeeds.
- Business theory like Porter's five forces is "all quite subjective" and can't be tested. He says he learned a thousand times more from eight years of doing than from university.
- If he were 18, he would skip university, go nomad and start businesses. He sees university mainly as a discipline test and a social experience.
- On stress: his late-20s breakdown peaked at 27, driven by fear of turning 30 unsuccessful. Therapy and getting the business working made him calmer and more autonomous.
- A million-dollar company means roughly 100k to 200k a year of revenue at a 5 to 10x multiple. He calls it "absolutely possible" for a solo app or website.

chunks.heading: Mindset: build solo, build to help, stay unattached
chunks.text:
- He builds alone: he writes the code, designs, makes the logo and database and does the marketing, and says you can change people's lives from a laptop.
- Not every project is monetized. He built an airline safety and route-map site (Airline List) partly because it was fun, and it filters for safe airlines.
- He values autonomy over your own decisions as a growing trend, linked to decentralization (crypto, censorship resistance), though he thinks the tech isn't ready yet.
- He ties impermanence and not clinging to things to being able to take risks like moving countries.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Levels explains why he builds one minimal MVP per month after a two-year project flopped with four free trial users. The monthly deadline forces him to finish and keep scope small, and the 12-in-12 narrative earns press coverage that drives users. He also covers sourcing ideas from his own problems, funding bigger goals with side-project cash flow, and not being intimidated by polished products.

chunks.heading: Why Pieter builds 12 startups in 12 months
chunks.text:
- He spent about two years perfecting one product and launched it to four free-trial users who then left. He calls it "horrible" after "I worked so hard on this."
- Building something every month forces him to finish things and keep them minimal. He says he has always procrastinated on finishing, and the deadline fixes that.
- The aim is to shift products faster and find out quickly which ones work, "like throwing spaghetti on the wall and seeing what sticks."
- He is candid that the label is partly "a marketing ploy." They are MVPs built in a Lean Startup spirit, not full startups. He built the site, got market fit if possible, monetized fast, then moved to the next.
- He argues most people share the same ideas ("we all have the same ideas and it's just about execution now"). He keeps a years-old Trello board with lists like plans, work in progress, complete failure and success, and drags ideas right until they finish or fail.

chunks.heading: How he builds fast and keeps the quality high
chunks.text:
- He does the front end and back end himself, so he says he cannot be great at anything in particular. Keeping things minimal makes them look clean and saves time, which gives a better design aesthetic.
- Ideas come mostly from his own problems. Nomad List came from not knowing which cities to work and travel from.
- He borrows layouts from existing sites. Nomad List took Product Hunt's list-based layout and applied it to cities, with modifications.
- Idea sourcing is roughly 50/50 between his backlog and actively hunting for the next one while building the current month's product.
- His advice against perfectionism: the customer only sees the finished product and never the mess behind it. "Just make it look as if it works and then that's enough." Everyone's back end is a mess, so don't be scared to build something because you think you can't.

chunks.heading: Revenue from the early projects
chunks.text:
- Most of the projects earned revenue at that point. He estimates about three of four or five were generating revenue actively.
- One site (a swear-word-titled domain, "effingdoit.com") earns completely automatically with no work from him.
- Nomad List was his most recent and most successful, monetized through simple ads: two paid advertisers for remote jobs. It ranks cities for working and living remotely by cost of living, weather and similar factors.

chunks.heading: Using a "12 in 12" narrative to get press
chunks.text:
- Press needs news and a spin. "They're not going to write about something that's common." Pieter says to build a narrative around your products or personality that genuinely fits you, because you can't fake it.
- He tried for ages to get coverage the year before, and it didn't work. Having a narrative made it much easier.
- The first contact was John Russell of The Next Web, who reached out because Pieter blogged about working on a startup from Chiang Mai, Thailand. After that he sent every new site to John, and the first covered was Go F*** and Do It.
- He considers press essential to getting users, even for non-tech products, because "everything is tech these days."
- The framing was partly luck: he wrote "12 projects in 12 months," then backspaced "projects" and typed "startups" as a joke. He admits it felt a little sleazy, but argues it is a delicate balance and that "startup" gives the dreamy feeling that something might become something.
- Each month's launch gives a new follow-up story, since the series builds a narrative over time.

chunks.heading: Handling criticism of "trivial" startups
chunks.text:
- A Wired journalist asked whether nomadic work in developing countries exploits people, and why he builds trivial first-world products.
- Pieter's view on travel: it is beneficial in the way tourism can be, with money coming into lower-income countries, helping create middle classes (he cites Thailand's tourism in the 80s and 90s) as long as it is done respectfully.
- He concedes the journalist has a point that builders sit in a Western bubble, and it inspired him to think about solving less trivial problems. He sees that as a long-term project, since he was 28 and just starting.
- His practical argument: you need cash flow to solve big problems. A person in a nine-to-five job should build their own products for monthly cash flow, then focus on something big.

chunks.heading: Focusing on the nomad market and what's next
chunks.text:
- His approach is to see which project sticks, and Nomad List was sticking. He saw it as a market he is part of: people selling homes and quitting rent to move to South America or Southeast Asia, which he sees as becoming a feasible lifestyle.
- He wants to remove friction in arriving somewhere new, such as SIM cards, transit cards and finding co-working, which can take days to sort out in a place like Bangkok.
- Planned projects: Giftbook, which prints animated GIFs as flipbooks shipped to your house (he searched and found nobody had done it, with only a competitor doing stereoscopic cards), and Nomad Kit, a bundle for arriving in a city (Austin, Chiang Mai, Bali) with co-working, hotel stay, SIM card, transit card and a guide.
- He expected more nomad-related projects among the 12.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a fireside with Balaji, Pieter Levels explains how he maintains Nomad List, Photo AI and other apps nearly alone. He favors scrappy, fast shipping on a stable vanilla PHP stack, with AI coding help, and builds features that solve real nomad pain. The rest of the talk covers digital nomad stats and network state debate.

chunks.heading: Digital nomads as a market: sizing and profile
chunks.text:
- Pieter presented a prediction about 9 years ago of 1 billion digital nomads by 2035. He says people called him crazy until Covid made remote work normal.
- His 2024 figures: about 13% of the world works remotely, roughly one billion people out of about three billion workers. He estimates 10-20% of remote workers are digital nomads, so about 100 to 200 million people working from other countries on and off, not full-time.
- A decade earlier this was a "micro subculture"; now it is massive.
- Profile from his Nomad List statistics page: most male nomads are software developers, most women work in marketing, and 66% are single.
- They are not poor backpackers. Average income is about $125,000 per year, 90% are university educated, and 34% hold a master's degree.
- He sees this as a very attractive, already-mobile, high-income audience for any "network state" that wants to collect taxes.

chunks.heading: Building data products from user statistics (Nomad List)
chunks.text:
- Nomad List has a statistics page inspired by OkCupid's dating statistics, which were removed after the match.com acquisition. It covers differences between men and women nomads, political leanings, diet (meat or vegan) and more.
- Example finding: about 75% of women digital nomads are progressive, versus about 45% of men. Few nomads are conservative.
- He maintains the data by hand ("Grind Mode on these spreadsheets") but only needs to refresh it about once a year, for example by downloading World Bank or IMF data and normalizing it.
- He notes that data sites that look simple are "deceptively hard". A passport index has about 200 countries squared, so about 40,000 cells that all must be right. His visa filter has the same problem, because rules change every few months (the EU recently added three countries to Schengen).

chunks.heading: Keeping a one-man portfolio of apps running
chunks.text:
- He runs Nomad List, Remote OK, Photo AI and several other AI apps largely alone, plus Daniel, a part-time server admin on an SLA who only comes online if the server dies and does Linux upgrades.
- His principle: be scrappy and ship fast, but never be sloppy on security. "You cannot do security wrong" because you hold user data.
- His stack is vanilla PHP. He argues it rarely changes, so there is little maintenance. Major PHP upgrades needed only small fixes, and he says the language is now professional.
- He starts with everything in one file and splits later. He writes vanilla code and improves it slowly.
- He now uses Cursor and other AI tools heavily to write code.
- On Photo AI, he notes the AI photos keep improving. His own face shows up in AI photos more often because they look a little better than real life.

chunks.heading: Product idea: alerts for tax residency and visa limits
chunks.text:
- Nomad List sends a bot message when a user is about to become tax liable in a country within the next 30 days. This works because users log their trips.
- He says users love it. Just before the 183-day or 90-day threshold, the bot says "get out of the country".
- Visa questions are a core need. Example: a Dutch person with a German girlfriend asks which countries they can visit.
- A related concept is the "perpetual traveler": rotate among about six countries every 60 days so you are not a tax resident of any of them. He sees that as an app idea, but notes the cost is difficulty keeping relationships and friends. He thinks it suits people in their 20s.

chunks.heading: Choosing where to live: friends first, economics second
chunks.text:
- He pushes back on moving somewhere just for 0% tax (such as Puerto Rico). His order: first pick a place that is actually nice to live, with your friends near you, and only then add tax benefits.
- He moved essentially all his friends to a beach village on the Portuguese coast, with friends five minutes away on foot. He says this changes your happiness completely.
- He observes nomad scenes split into different tribes over time: Bangkok differs from Bali, and Canggu is more Western. During Covid there were "ski nomads" who moved to US ski villages to snowboard and work remotely.
- He notes you can now either move to where your people are, or find your people online and then move.

chunks.heading: Ambition and culture as a location factor
chunks.text:
- He says Europe feels less ambitious than Asia. In northern Europe he cites a "Jante's law"-style attitude (Danish/Swedish: "you think you're better than us").
- If you start a business in Europe, people "immediately look for the problems"; in Asia people say "let's start a business."
- He sees a brain drain from Europe: founders move to the UK, US or Asia because regulation is heavy.
- He made the "make Europe great again" hat as a joke to push Europe toward being better for startups. He prefers iterating on what you have over resetting from zero, and would like founders to move back.
- He notes that when he deregistered from the Netherlands, it felt scary, as if he were an "international vigilante". He observes governments cultivate that fear, and cites exit taxes such as Norway's.

chunks.heading: Crypto payments and the network state critique
chunks.text:
- He owns crypto but does not use it daily, so he is "not completely convinced yet". He also questions the physical "declare a state" final step of the network state concept, asking who will actually show up, and noting a proposed Egypt-Sudan network state would need both countries.
- On payments, Balaji urged building crypto wallets into products. Pieter's practical objection: it is hard to implement because he already runs Stripe, and supporting multiple processors is a burden. He suggested users can use a Coinbase card instead.
- Balaji advised re-evaluating every three to six months, since USDC on Solana and Base now enable micropayments. Pieter noted Stripe has added crypto and he is waiting for it to appear in the "enable payment methods" settings.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a short fireside chat at SafetyWing's summit, Levels recounts how timing and circumstance (faster internet, a Dutch graduate priced out of Holland) led him into nomad startups. He argues the nomad niche has split into subgroups as its users age, that European institutions and startups are too slow, and that the opportunity now lies in services for settled, relocating people.

chunks.heading: Why Pieter started as a digital nomad: cost, tech timing, and building startups
chunks.text:
- Pieter began traveling in 2013 after graduating in Brazil. He did not know the term "digital nomad" yet.
- Holland was too expensive to stay and build startups on his limited money and savings, so he went to Asia.
- He credits "a lot of coincidences": internet was just becoming fast enough to work from a laptop on the other side of the world (Skype did not work in Bali in 2014, only from 2017), and he was a new graduate who wanted to build startups rather than get a normal job.
- He blogged and tweeted about it, which pulled the idea into the developer and programmer world while it was still "very nascent."

chunks.heading: How the digital nomad market has split into subgroups
chunks.text:
Pieter says the single backpack-and-laptop niche of 10+ years ago has fragmented. The people who were 25 are now 35, often with kids, and want to do it their own way.

- **Settled nomads:** many stopped traveling and settled in places other than where they were born (he lives in a beach town in Portugal, "very like hippie and chill, kind of like Bali"; others choose Costa Rica). Some homeschool, live in eco villages, or grow food.
- **Crypto and Bitcoin people:** have their own nomad space.
- **Network states:** such as Prospera, are popular, especially with crypto people. He notes Switzerland seems to be starting something similar.
- **Young people in their 20s:** travel and work remotely "without even knowing it" because they grew up with the internet. For example, Americans bring a laptop to Spain or Portugal and stay for months.

He says he is thinking of giving another presentation, in person, on where this goes next.

chunks.heading: What startups to build now: services for settling nomads and migrants
chunks.text:
Pieter's advice on where the opportunity is:

- Look less at the nomads of 10 years ago and more at settling nomads looking for the most attractive place to live.
- The decision factors he lists: taxes, wealth, entrepreneurship and business climate, free speech, health care, safety, clean streets, how good it is to raise kids, education, and whether international schools exist.
- Build services that get these people to those places and help them move.
- He says companies helping people migrate already exist and it is "a big market. If you want to jump in there, for sure."
- Health care is an essential component: "You don't want to be in a foreign country and you can't go to the hospital and you can't pay for it."

chunks.heading: Why remote work is now normal, and why top talent keeps freedom
chunks.text:
- COVID normalized remote work. Before, it was "very strange or fringy"; after, everybody had done it and knew it worked.
- Companies are now pushing people back to the office (often hybrid), but people prefer freedom.
- Top talent keeps its freedom because it can choose where to work. He points to top AI talent, who "can work with however they want to be because they are so important and so valuable."

chunks.heading: Pieter's view on Europe: no startups, high regulation, and slow government
chunks.text:
- Having lived in Asia for about 10 years, then returning to Portugal during COVID, he says some things in Europe are better: clean air, more freedom and democracy, and free speech in theory.
- Much is behind: it is "not modern" or convenient, and there are hardly any startups. He says no European company is in the top 25 by market cap and there are no big European tech companies.
- European founders move to San Francisco to raise money and never come back, so "Europe is not benefiting from startup economies at all. They educate and raise."
- Rather than only complain, he started tweeting solutions and crowdsourcing ideas. People then asked him for advice, and he talked to the ex-prime minister of Italy and the ex-director of the European Central Bank, whose report included his feedback.
- He says change is very slow and he has not seen results yet.

chunks.heading: Why Pieter thinks network states and places like Dubai are gaining ground
chunks.text:
- He ties his bullishness on network states to a tweet about people, especially founders from the UK, moving to Dubai.
- He says Dubai has a bad reputation in Europe, but he has been there and "things are pretty good": people seem happy and there is a lot of business and entrepreneur activity.
- In Europe he sees higher taxes, more regulation, more censorship (Germany, Britain), and slow health care with waiting lists of 9 months to 2 years for certain operations. His view: "If you're paying into this system, you're not getting rewarded anymore."
- He frames network states less as new countries and more as places like Dubai, special economic zones, and Portugal that attract entrepreneurs and foreigners with money to spend. Qatar, Dubai and Singapore run in "a more rational way": how to make the best service for citizens.
- His tension: startups move fast and governments move slowly, so they "don't go together."
- He still values democracy and free speech and prefers to live where he can "say whatever I want" without going to jail, noting that many top-performing countries are autocratic monarchies.

chunks.heading: What a global safety net should provide
chunks.text:
When asked what the most important feature is, Pieter says:

- Emergency care first: if something happens, he wants to reach a local hospital wherever he lives or travels and get the best care possible.
- Due process like any other service: claims handled fast, with money paid quickly so he can cover bills wherever he is in the world.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Pieter Levels talks with SafetyWing's Sondre about how remote work is going mainstream, why he stays bootstrapped, and why meaning comes from people rather than aesthetics. He explains how Nomad List started as a fix for his own problem and which problems remote workers still need solved.

chunks.heading: Remote work will turn some home-workers into nomads, and the 1 billion nomads prediction
chunks.text:
- Pieter's 2015 prediction was 1 billion digital nomads by 2035, driven by cheap air travel, more freelancers, remote workers, the sharing economy and better internet. The prediction predates his later work, but he still stands by it.
- His definition is loose: a remote worker who works from outside their home country for at least part of the year. He says full "bouncing around from city to city every week" nomads are rare, and "people go crazy if you do that".
- Evidence he cites: he says about 70% of startup teams in Silicon Valley were part or mostly remote when they started out. Regular companies were forced into remote work by Corona.
- His logic for the transition: first people work from home, then from cafes, then from another city, then from another country. He did this himself while finishing his thesis in San Francisco and running a YouTube music channel.
- His estimate: perhaps 5-10% of work-from-home remote workers will make the jump. On a US labor force of 150-200 million, that is roughly 20 million people potentially working from other cities or countries.
- He points to "Zoom towns" (remote workers moving to smaller towns and booking Airbnbs) as the early sign.

chunks.heading: Why Nomad List exists: solving his own problem with criteria quality-of-life rankings ignore
chunks.text:
- Nomad List started as a personal problem in about 2014, when he was nomading through Chiang Mai, Bangkok and Vietnam. These places did not appear in typical quality-of-life rankings, which favor Scandinavia and Vienna.
- He set criteria specific to remote workers: internet speed, safety, weather (mild or warm), and cost.
- He collected the data and ranked cities against it. Later he added social data, so the ranking reflects whether other nomads actually live there and whether you can make friends or find community.
- His principle: with a laptop-based life, the places that win are the ones with a community of similar people, not just good infrastructure.
- Pattern worth noting: he built a product by picking a problem from his own life and quantifying the criteria nobody else measured.

chunks.heading: Company culture: half-remote doesn't work
chunks.text:
- He agrees with David Heinemeier Hansson and Matt Mullenweg that hybrid companies (some people in the office, some remote) have a cultural problem. Remote people are left out of social gatherings that can't be replicated online.
- His view: a company should be either a physical-office company or fully remote.
- He expects many regular companies, such as the Dutch ones he sees, to drift back to a split team after lockdowns and hit this problem.

chunks.heading: Fringe to mainstream: how remote work went from a subculture to normal
chunks.text:
- Five years earlier remote work and nomadism got huge pushback and were a "fringe subculture". Interviewer's company had to hide being remote from investors in 2016; by 2020 it was a plus.
- His insight: debates and arguments don't decide adoption. "You can always find arguments against things when that's not your culture. But then when the culture changes, you're like, 'Okay, I'll do it, too.'"
- Every fringe subculture has the potential to go mainstream, and early adopters should expect resistance at first.
- He compares it to underground drum and bass: a scene either becomes mainstream or dies out. A business built on a counterculture needs it to grow, even though growth costs the "romantic" early feeling.
- Startups work the same way: you start something because it is missing from the market and culture, you push it, and by pushing it you create the market.
- Consequence for him: he has to find the next fringe thing, which he says he hadn't worked out yet and might take 5-10 years.

chunks.heading: Bootstrapping versus venture funding
chunks.text:
- He has never raised funding or taken bank loans. Revenue goes back into the business, and mostly into food and coffee so he can code more. He avoids hiring and uses only short-term contracts.
- Exit odds argument: he cites odds of roughly 0-10% for a startup exit. If a startup takes about 5 years, "you'd need to be doing startups for 50 years to get one exit".
- On VCs: he says most VC funds return less than an S&P 500 ETF, VCs earn on management fees (he gives roughly 3-5% per year, e.g. $5 million a year on a $100 million fund), and pension funds put around 10% of their money into high-risk venture portfolios because they need the exposure.
- His advice: unless you have a really unfair advantage, start small and bootstrap.
- Market signal: when bootstrapped, anything you change shows up immediately in revenue, a very direct connection to the market. With VC money in the bank there is little incentive to build revenue early, so "you can do a lot of BS as a startup".
- He says he could raise VC money on his revenue now but would rather reinvest it himself.
- Valuation note: a website broker told him he typically pays three to four to five times annual revenue. Founders think their product is special; to the market it is a normal business. He wouldn't sell Nomad List: "It's my baby".

chunks.heading: Why people go nomad, and what is still unsolved
chunks.text:
- His reasons: it became possible, boredom with a routine 9-to-5, wanting different cultures and adventures in his 20s, and the chance to be around people who fit you better than your birthplace's community does.
- Purpose-based moves: anime fans to Japan, jiu-jitsu fighters to Brazil, snowboarders to ski towns (Lake Tahoe, Denver, Boulder), surfers to surf towns. He expects cities to differentiate more by interest, self-reinforcing.
- Waves: first wave around 2007 (Tim Ferriss), second around 2014, third after Corona.
- Startup requests he names:
  - Kids' education for nomad families: central online coursework from a certified provider (e.g. Harvard), plus affiliated local schools running the practical classes with other kids. Nomad parents often want alternatives like Montessori.
  - Community building. Even slowmading between Bali and Seoul makes friendships harder than staying in one place for 20 years.
  - Facilitating remote work hubs physically with services, which he calls a good business, though he isn't sure of the form.
- Against building villages: he says communes in the 1960s often broke up from infighting, and he doesn't think privately built villages or castles work. He recommends iterating on existing places: build roots in a hub, open a school, a nice co-working space or cafe, and "make sure the money goes back to locals".
- Hubs form organically: he felt the closest to this in Canggu (Bali), a bit in Chiang Mai, and cites Tulum. He expects nomad hubs to become remote work hubs, and doesn't think artificial places will work.

chunks.heading: Happiness, meaningful work and picking projects
chunks.text:
- He argues the lifestyle marketing around nomadism (infinity pools, beaches, "buy this course for $3,000") is boring in practice and is essentially materialism, as is Instagram experientialism.
- What he says actually makes people happy: the right people around you, meaningful work, health and sports, therapy, and flow from making things.
- Meaningful work doesn't have to be the main job. Volunteer work, even online (building a website for a library), can supply it.
- His own path: music was most meaningful but had weak market fit ("I wasn't good probably enough"). He then built sites to solve his own problems, which made them meaningful. He calls it partly luck that his money-making products are also meaningful.
- Nomad List is more meaningful to him; Remote OK is "more boring, but it's very necessary" as a job board for remote jobs.
- His advice: don't focus on finding perfectly meaningful work as your main job, since market fit is hard. Find meaning first from people.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Pieter Levels lays out a 10-point playbook for building a startup with no funding: solve your own problem, ship ugly fast, charge from day 1, use boring tech and cheap hosting, do support yourself, automate, build in public, and keep burn near zero. He frames VC as a game that makes founders think they need permission.

chunks.heading: Core principle: start with your own problem and ship ugly fast
chunks.text:
- Pieter says to "pick a problem you personally have." His test: "if you don't use your own product daily, quit now."
- He skips the pitch deck. He opens the code editor and ships "something ugly in a weekend."
- He argues the VC game is built to make founders think they need permission to start. His view: "you don't."

chunks.heading: Monetization: charge from day 1
chunks.text:
- He says to charge money from day 1.
- His reason: "free users give you nothing but support tickets."
- Paying customers are the validation. Free users don't give a meaningful signal.

chunks.heading: Tech stack and hosting: boring and cheap
chunks.text:
- He recommends boring tech: PHP, SQLite, vanilla JS.
- He calls frameworks "a trap that mass waste your time."
- He hosts on a cheap VPS at $5-20/mo, not AWS.
- His reasoning: "you don't need kubernetes for 1,000 users."

chunks.heading: Operations: do support yourself, automate the rest
chunks.text:
- He does customer support himself because "it's the fastest product feedback loop that exists."
- He automates "everything you do more than twice."
- His rule: "cron jobs > employees."

chunks.heading: Distribution: build in public on X
chunks.text:
- He grows on Twitter/X by building in public.
- His framing: "your journey IS the marketing."
- The essay itself reached 646,370 views and 12,660 likes on X, an example of the channel he describes.

chunks.heading: Financial independence: near-zero burn, no equity deals
chunks.text:
- He keeps burn rate near zero so he never needs to raise. His phrase: "ramen profitable > series A."
- He says no to investors, cofounders and "advisors" who want equity for intros.
- He reports 10+ years of working this way with no employees, no funding and no board meetings.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Levels explains his 12-startups workflow: solve your own problems, keep sites minimal, own the whole stack on one cheap VPS, skip frameworks and databases, and deploy a new site in about 15 minutes. His core message is that tools matter less than being fast and comfortable with what you know.

chunks.heading: Pieter's MVP philosophy: ship fast, rough, and minimal
chunks.text:
- Pieter says the #1 question about his "12 startups in 12 months" challenge is how he ships so fast. His answer: "I do work fast and rough," not longer hours.
- He warns that he doesn't do things conventionally, so copying him exactly is a bad idea. Better to figure out your own workflow.
- He starts by scratching his own itch (a DHH phrase). Examples: GoFuckingDoIt (fines him if he doesn't finish what he said he would), Tubelytics (overview of his YouTube channels' performance), NomadList (which cities have the best cost of living for a traveling nomad).
- Solving your own problems is a good start, but it limits audience and problem settings. In the long run he wants to build things with a wider impact.
- "I'm not [a programmer] and I don't want to be one either. I just want my stuff to work and not break." Making stuff is his passion, not programming, like liking how math builds a skyscraper.
- His sites are minimal on purpose. He doesn't see the point of building big immediately and doesn't think a site needs functionality from top to bottom.
- If something takes off, he wants the code readable enough for others to refactor or scale.
- Conclusion: tools don't matter. PHP, Node, Ruby: "It's really about what you're best, quickest and most comfortable with."

chunks.heading: Design and front-end workflow
chunks.text:
- He usually has the look in his head and sketches it on paper first (GoFuckingDoIt's first sketch "looks terrible").
- Next he builds it in Photoshop, then in HTML and CSS, where the design keeps evolving. The name changed from Just Fucking Do It to Go Fucking Do It and the photo was swapped.
- For stock photos he gets a mock (watermarked comp) from Stocksy first, and pays $10 for the license only once he decides to use it.
- He tweaks until the interface looks great, then makes it responsive using Chrome's emulation. 40% of his traffic came from mobile at the time, and "People will simply leave your site if they can't use it."
- Front-end comes first. The back-end and interactivity come after.

chunks.heading: Dev environment
chunks.text:
- No IDE. He codes in Sublime Text 3 (auto-completion, linting, dark themes such as Soda), plus CodeKit to compile and minify JS and SCSS and surface errors.
- Earlier he had no local server. He uploaded every change to a DreamHost dev server to test, which took "1000x more time."
- He recommends a Mac because OS X resembles Linux, so the dev machine nearly duplicates the production server. He can code and test offline without breaking the live site.

chunks.heading: Hosting and tech stack
chunks.text:
- He moved from shared hosting (DreamHost) to his own Linode VPS after heavy cron jobs drew complaints. Setting it up took about a week and he didn't know the Linux shell then.
- Owning the whole stack means he can find problems quickly instead of debugging for 12 hours only to find the host's fault.
- Stack: Nginx + PHP-FPM on Ubuntu 14.04 LTS on Linode, with PHP, Node.js, hand-coded HTML, raw JS with jQuery, and some SCSS/raw CSS.
- All his sites, including the blog, run on one VPS costing $40/month (4 GB RAM, 4 CPU cores, 96 GB SSD, 4 TB transfer). It handles Hacker News and Product Hunt floods (often >1000 concurrent users) and has never gone down except when he broke it.
- He prefers Linode's simplicity to AWS: a server is deployed with one button and running in 5 minutes.
- He admits PHP is embarrassing to say but it has improved, and he feels pressure to move to Node.

chunks.heading: Deploying a new site in about 15 minutes
chunks.text:
1. Register the domain at NameCheap and use FreeDNS to point it at the VPS IP.
2. Clone an nginx.conf from another domain and tweak it.
3. Upload it, SSH in, symlink it into Nginx's sites folder and reload Nginx:
   - `sudo ln -s /srv/http/domain.com/app/nginx.conf /etc/nginx/sites/domain.com`
   - `sudo nginx -s restart`

- SSH beats hosting web panels, which used to take him hours per new domain.

chunks.heading: Folder structure and coding style
chunks.text:
- `/_assets`: mockups, logos, press screenshots, anything not for the server.
- `/public/assets/`: publicly served CSS, JS and images, pre-processed from `/app/`.
- `/app/`: front-end and back-end code plus nginx.conf, which acts as the router to specific PHP files. Only `/public/` is web-accessible.
- `/lib/`: third-party libraries (Stripe, Twitter OAuth).
- `/workers/`: cron-scheduled background jobs (email queues, scraping, backups).
- `/logs/`: plain .txt output, e.g. a cron redirected to `logs/doStuff.txt`.
- `/data/`: JSON text files instead of a database, named with an MD5 hash (NomadList: city + state + country).
- He admits the no-database approach is horrible but fast, and hates designing schemas before knowing the fields. You can script a move to MySQL/PostgreSQL later, but use a proper database for sensitive user data.
- He uses no frameworks except jQuery ("many times, they just make things more complex"). He follows DRY and KISS, and reuses code from previous projects.

chunks.heading: Task management with Trello
chunks.text:
- He had trouble getting tasks done. His Trello board has lists for this year, this month, this week, today, and now (copied from a Hacker News commenter).
- He drags the current task into "now" for focus, then into a completed list on its left.
- Each week's finished list moves to a "finished" board. Looking back at weeks of finished work gives satisfaction and a loose measure of productivity.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Levels explains his 2014 challenge to launch one startup per month. He diagnoses creatives' two killers, not finishing and fear of launching, and argues for starting small, exposing yourself to market forces, and defining a startup as a new product that grows fast.

chunks.heading: Why Pieter set the 12 startups in 12 months challenge
chunks.text:
- Pieter took inspiration from Jennifer Dewalt's "180 websites in 180 days". Unlike her, he could already build, so his goal was to practice finishing and launching.
- Goal (March 2014): launch one startup every month for 12 months. Each month covers picking an idea, developing it, and launching it to press.
- He described it as "a tiny personal hyperfast incubator" meant to change his habits and force him to finish what he starts.
- His expectation: after 12 months he would have more to show for his name.
