chunks.heading: The two problems: finishing and launching
chunks.text:
- **Finishing:** creatives (musicians, writers, developers) are perfectionists, and projects are never "just done". There is always one more feature or chapter. Near the finish line they drop the project and move to something new, because "we like the feeling of starting something 'new', we despise the feeling of finishing something 'old'."
- **Launching:** fear of failure keeps builders from launching. They hold a perfect fantasy of press coverage and signups that reality will not match, so they under-launch or never launch. His reasoning: "what if anybody would actually use what we built? They might hate it!"
- **Result:** a vicious cycle of no progress. He had seen startups with great ideas and long hours still sitting on the same landing page collecting beta emails a year later.
- He had suffered from both problems himself for years, and he saw them killing good ideas in others too.

chunks.heading: Why small projects count as startups
chunks.text:
- Pieter argues a startup does not have to be a "world changing high impact $1B+ company from the start". He calls that a myth.
- Examples he cites: Airbnb started as a company selling Obama-themed cereal. Dropbox started as Drew Houston building a graphical user interface for rsync as a side project. The big vision came after they found market fit with their MVPs.
- Waiting for a big vision while staying idle is the wrong approach. Doing something puts you ahead of most people, and "you'll probably do the wrong thing. But that's not the point."
- You learn by exposing yourself to the world and its market forces: "By doing nothing, you figure out exactly nothing."
- Especially if you are inexperienced, start small first and slowly build bigger things.

chunks.heading: His definition of a startup and the one-month test
chunks.text:
- He combined Eric Ries's definition (a human institution delivering a new product or service under extreme uncertainty) with Paul Graham's (a company designed to grow fast, where growth is the only essential thing).
- His minified definition: "A startup delivers a new product and grows it fast."
- Delivering a new product is the easy part; growing it fast is the hard part. It gets tougher if there is no market fit after the MVP.
- His rule: see whether a project gets market fit within one month. If it shows no signs of being somewhat in demand, he considers it failed and moves on.

chunks.heading: What he shipped as the progress report
chunks.text:
His list of projects at the time of writing:

1. **Play My Inbox:** collects music from people's inboxes and playlists it in a visual music player.
2. **Go Fucking Do It:** forces you to reach goals by a deadline, and charges your card if you do not.
3. **Tubelytics:** a real-time analytics dashboard SaaS for YouTube publishers and media brands, tracking hundreds of channels, videos and networks.
4. **NomadList:** a live index of the best cities to live and work remotely, scored on cost of living, weather, internet speed and crowdsourced metrics. It sells city guide books and nomad kits (coworking day pass, SIM card, hotel stay).
5. **NomadJobs:** a job board for remote workers, featuring only 100% distributed startups such as Buffer, Zapier, Sqwiggle and Automattic.
6. **GifBook:** upload animated GIFs and order printed flip books made from them.
7. **#nomads:** a chat community for digital nomads. It had over 2,000 members, meet-ups from Berlin to Bangkok, and a Product Hunt feature.
8. **Remote | OK:** a daily aggregator of remote jobs. It does not accept job postings and is not curated. It aims to win on volume, indexing jobs from other boards and using sentiment analysis to decide whether they are remote. It reached #1 on Product Hunt.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Pieter Levels shares that only 4 of his 70+ projects ever made money and grew, meaning over 95% failed. His takeaway is that a ~5% hit rate is normal, so the way to win is to ship many projects.

chunks.heading: Pieter's hit rate: roughly 5%, so the answer is to ship more
chunks.text:
- Pieter reports that only 4 out of 70+ projects he has ever made earned money and grew.
- More than 95% of everything he made failed.
- He puts his hit rate at about 5%.
- His conclusion is short: "So...ship more."

chunks.heading: Treat failure as the normal outcome of building
chunks.text:
- Pieter does not present failure as a rare event to avoid. He presents it as the base rate: roughly 19 out of 20 projects do not work.
- The post was written in November 2021, and he counted 70+ projects at that point.
- He frames the numbers as a plain statement of fact, not a story of regret.

chunks.heading: Volume is the strategy
chunks.text:
- Since he cannot predict which project will be one of the few winners, he argues the way to find them is to make many projects.
- A low hit rate is acceptable when each attempt is cheap and fast to ship.
- The implication he draws is "ship more": more attempts mean more chances to land one of the roughly 5% that grow.

chunks.heading: Why this matters for a would-be founder
chunks.text:
- Failed projects do not define the outcome. The few that made money did, according to his own track record.
- He measures success by projects that "made money and grew," not by how many he started.
- His position is that the only way to improve the odds of a hit is to increase the number of shipped attempts.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Levels shares a milestone snapshot: after 4 years, two apps (Nomad List and Remote OK) reached $83k+/month, or $1M annualized, with no ad budget and no funding. The stats show a lean setup: one VPS, 208 cron jobs, and about 740 payments per month at a $115 average.

chunks.heading: $83,333/mo revenue milestone: where Nomad List and Remote OK stood after 4 years
chunks.text:
- In May 2019 Pieter announced that his two apps, Nomad List and Remote OK, had reached "$83,333+/mo revenue".
- He called $83k "special because * 12 is $1M", meaning $1M annual revenue.
- It took 4 years to get there.
- The snapshot: 11,996 customers, 740 payments per month, 208 cron jobs, $115 average payment, 2 apps, 1 VPS, $0 ad budget, $0 funding.
- The post got roughly 766k estimated views and 3,287 likes on X.

chunks.heading: The business model behind the number: few payments, high average ticket
chunks.text:
- 740 payments per month at a $115 average payment is what produces roughly $83k/mo.
- The $115 average payment is high for consumer web products, so a modest count of payments is enough to reach $1M a year.
- The 11,996 customers figure shows the base built up over the 4 years.
- Pieter presents the two apps as the whole business: `nomadlist.com` and `remoteok.io`.

chunks.heading: Lean infrastructure: one VPS and 208 cron jobs
chunks.text:
- The entire revenue base ran on 1 VPS.
- It used 208 cron jobs, which he lists as part of the stack alongside the 2 apps.
- Pieter treats this as a point of pride: a $1M/yr business with minimal servers and tooling.
- This fits his stated approach in the book *MAKE* of building startups without funding.

chunks.heading: Zero ad budget, zero funding
chunks.text:
- He reached the milestone with "0 ad budget": no paid acquisition.
- He reached it with "0 funding": no investors, fully bootstrapped.
- Both are listed in the same stat block as the revenue figures, as part of the achievement rather than as footnotes.
- He frames the 4-year timeline as the cost of doing it this way.

chunks.heading: Takeaways Pieter highlights
chunks.text:
- Slow, compounding progress: the $1M run rate took 4 years, across two products rather than one.
- Running multiple small apps on shared simple infrastructure can add up to seven figures a year.
- High per-payment value ($115 average) matters more than payment volume.
- No ads and no funding are presented as the baseline, not a handicap.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Levels explains how relentlessly cutting costs, including replacing SaaS tools by vibecoding his own, produced a 94.5% profit margin. The savings were invested in ETFs and a few startup bets, so investment returns now exceed his stable $200K-$250K/mo business revenue.

chunks.heading: Revenue stays flat while profit margin and investment returns do the compounding
chunks.text:
- Pieter passed $10M/y in combined revenue and investment gains in 2026, at a profit margin of about 94.5%.
- His business revenue has been very stable at about $200K-$250K/mo.
- Investment returns have now surpassed business revenue, which he says has been true for about a year.
- His loop: "Spend less -> lower costs -> more profit -> more money saved -> more money to invest -> more % returns on investments".
- Most gains are unrealized because he never sells, and he flags that investments fluctuate, so the figure deserves "a big grain of salt".

chunks.heading: Cutting SaaS dependencies by vibecoding replacements
chunks.text:
- Pieter has aggressively increased his profit margin for years, especially in the last few.
- This year he reduced his SaaS dependencies to just a handful of companies by vibecoding his own replacements.
- The result is the roughly 94.5% profit margin.
- He treats cost reduction as a first-class lever, equal to growing revenue.

chunks.heading: Investing profits: ETFs plus bets on suppliers he actually uses
chunks.text:
- Most of his investments are simple ETFs, such as the Vanguard S&P500.
- Alongside those he made a few stock and startup bets that worked out.
- 2022: he couldn't get any available GPUs, reasoned there was a shortage, and bought Nvidia.
- 2023: Danny Postma recommended investing in the companies behind the AI inference for their photo AI apps. He invested first in Replicate and then in FAL.
- 2025: he invested in Cursor, which was then acquired by SpaceX recently.
- His tactic: "I just asked every app/service I used if I could invest".
- The pattern is to invest in the tools and vendors he depends on and sees demand for firsthand.

chunks.heading: Staying lean and profitable instead of spending to grow
chunks.text:
- Many people over the last decade told him to spend all his money, personally or in the business, to grow it.
- He says he doesn't know how that would have ended up, and maybe his companies would be bigger.
- He is happy he took his "own lean profitable healthy way" and thinks it ended up great.

chunks.heading: Tracking profit margin and sleep next to revenue
chunks.text:
- He keeps revenue and investment gains, profit margin, sleep score and last workout together in a "situation monitor" dashboard.
- He says these are "equally important", treating health metrics as on par with financial ones.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Pieter Levels shares that Photoai.com runs as one 40,870-line index.php file and generates $105,000/mo revenue with $80,000/mo profit. The post is a short data point showing a very simple stack can support a high-margin AI business.

chunks.heading: Photoai.com's scale and revenue (March 2026)
chunks.text:
- Pieter reports that photoai.com is a single file called `index.php` with 40,870 lines.
- It makes $105,000/mo in revenue and $80,000/mo in profit, per his post dated 6 March 2026.
- Implied margin from his figures: $80,000 profit on $105,000 revenue, so about $25,000/mo goes to costs.
- The post is deliberately minimal: the headline numbers are the whole message.

chunks.heading: Architecture: one PHP file as the whole product
chunks.text:
- Pieter runs a profitable AI product from one monolithic PHP file rather than a framework, microservices or a multi-repo setup.
- The point he makes is that code structure and "clean architecture" are not what produce revenue. The product making $80,000/mo profit is a 40,870 line `index.php`.
- This matches his broader approach of building startups without funding, which he wrote up in his book MAKE.

chunks.heading: Takeaway for builders
chunks.text:
- Choose the simplest stack that ships (plain PHP, a single file) and let revenue, not engineering aesthetics, decide when to refactor.
- A large, unglamorous codebase is not a blocker to strong profit: he cites $80,000/mo profit from it.
- Share concrete numbers publicly (revenue and profit) as proof. The post reached 1,560,497 views, 7,250 likes and 501 reposts on X.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Pieter Levels shares that RemoteOK.io runs on one PHP file, index.php, and earned $2,342.04 in a single day. The post argues that a minimal stack with no frameworks or libraries can still produce serious revenue.

chunks.heading: RemoteOK's single-file architecture
chunks.text:
- Pieter states that RemoteOK.io is "a single PHP file called 'index.php'" that generated $2,342.04 in one day (post dated 7 December 2017).
- He says it uses "No frameworks. No libraries."
- The point he is making: a profitable product does not require a framework, a dependency stack, or a complex architecture. A single file handled the whole site and earned over $2,300 in a day.

chunks.heading: Building simple to make money
chunks.text:
- Pieter presents the single-file setup as a deliberate strength and celebrates it ("💖"), not as a limitation to apologize for.
- The post is a signal that revenue comes from the product and its distribution, not from technical sophistication.
- This is consistent with his book MAKE, which he describes as being about "building startups without funding."

chunks.heading: Specific revenue figure as proof
chunks.text:
- He quotes revenue to the cent ($2,342.04) for a single day, a pattern of showing exact numbers in public to make the claim credible.
- The post drew roughly 381,916 estimated views, 1,639 likes and 645 reposts on X, showing how sharing real revenue and a contrarian tech choice drives attention to the product.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Pieter Levels advises against going full time on a side project right away. Build it while you have stable job income, and only consider quitting once the project's revenue has exceeded your salary for six consecutive months.

chunks.heading: Don't quit until side project revenue beats your job for 6 months
chunks.text:
- Pieter says many people quit their job and go full time on a side project, and he wouldn't recommend it.
- His alternative is a two-step rule:
  - Build the side project while you have stable income from a job.
  - Consider quitting only when the side project's revenue has surpassed your job's income for 6 months.
- The core principle is to keep a stable salary while the project is still unproven, and let revenue, not enthusiasm, trigger the decision to go full time.

chunks.heading: The revenue trigger: exceed job income, sustained for 6 months
chunks.text:
- The threshold is relative to the job: side project revenue must exceed what the job pays, not merely become "meaningful".
- The 6-month duration matters. A single strong month does not count; the revenue has to stay above job income for a full 6 months before quitting is even worth considering.
- Even at that point he only says to "consider quitting", not to quit automatically.

chunks.heading: Why he builds while employed rather than going all-in
chunks.text:
- Pieter advises building the project "while you have stable income from a job", which keeps financial pressure low while you test whether the product works.
- This fits his wider bootstrapping approach, described in his book MAKE, of building startups without funding.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Levels explains why press spikes decay and how a loosely branded community keeps users coming back. He seeded a Slack chat with authorities, rolled it out gradually, launched publicly, and hit 300+ members in 24 hours. The community doubles as a user focus group, launch channel and marketing engine.

chunks.heading: Building a community to retain users after press spikes
chunks.text:
- Pieter's problem: press coverage (e.g. Nomad List's launch) creates traffic spikes, then users leave and the tail slopes downwards.
- His fix is a community around the product's audience, which keeps bringing people back.
- A community "sticks a lot longer than press coverage". Once engaged, it can be turned into users for whatever product he pushes at that moment.
- He argues that "the hardest part of startups these days is not building the product or app. It's getting people to actually use what you built."

chunks.heading: A community doesn't need to be a forum or tied to your brand
chunks.text:
- A community can be informal. It need not be a forum, discussion board, comments section, social network, or even on your own site.
- Example he cites: Ryan Hoover building Product Hunt by personally engaging users on Twitter and inviting product makers to comment when their products appeared on the site.
- A following can form organically. Press focused disproportionately on Pieter working remotely. He knew he needed a narrative for press, embraced it, and it gave him a following of people into remote working.
- Platforms can be Twitter, Slack, in-app, or in real life through meetups.
- For Nomad List he kept branding subtle: only the logo, and the name #nomads instead of Nomad List. The community targets the site's audience (digital nomads and aspiring ones), not only current users, and is only loosely tied to the brand.

chunks.heading: Launching the #nomads Slack: seed, test, roll out, then announce
chunks.text:
Step by step, as Pieter did it in 2014:
1. Identify an audience that already exists but isn't connected. People tweeted and emailed him daily, but didn't know each other.
2. Set up a Slack chat with subtle branding.
3. Seed top-down: first invite authorities in the remote community who knew him and Nomad List (Amit Gupta of Photojojo, John O'Nolan of Ghost, James Seymour-Lock of Simple As Milk).
4. Test for a few weeks, then invite more people each week.
5. About a month later, launch publicly with a tweet and a nice picture ("open to new members until midnight EST", 27 October 2014).
6. Since Slack needs manual invites, link a Typeform sign-up form to Slack to auto-invite.

His view on quality: "quantity != quality", but seeding the right type of people from the start helps keep the base high quality.

chunks.heading: Results and a second launch on Product Hunt and Hacker News
chunks.text:
- Within 24 hours: 300+ members and 5,000+ messages. He couldn't keep up with sending invites.
- Conversations organized themselves around cities (#chiang-mai, #bali) plus the main #nomads channel. Derivatives appeared on other platforms (a Sqwiggle room, an impromptu video chat).
- A competing nomad chat (NomadNet) pointed its members to #nomads because it was growing faster.
- A few days later he built a quick landing page at hashtagnomads.com and submitted it to Product Hunt and Hacker News. It passed Microsoft's Band there and pushed the community to 500+ members, adding tech people interested in nomadism.
- By December 2014 the community was almost 1,500 users.

chunks.heading: Keeping spam out and the community inclusive
chunks.text:
- With spammers and predatory HR recruiters arriving, he added a $15 to $25 price for new sign-ups (depending on how popular the chat is) as an artificial limit on growth.
- He deliberately seeded with people aware of sexism, aiming for a gender-positive community. Past nomad communities were often male-dominated ("bromads").
- His reasoning: he wants everybody to become a nomad, so the community must be "highly inclusive, non-threatening and inviting to everybody."
- He appointed a diverse group of moderators and admins.

chunks.heading: Why a community pays off: user research, launches, and IRL meetups
chunks.text:
- Free user focus group: he sees what the audience talks about, what their problems are, can ask what they want built, and gets feedback while building.
- Launch channel: new products or features can be launched instantly to the community for users and feedback.
- IRL: city channels spawned meetup talk within a week. He made them official Nomad List meetups. The first, in Berlin, was organized by David Nagy. Others were planned in Montreal, Chiang Mai, Phuket, Hong Kong and Bali, and anyone can sign up to organize one.
- Meetups are a natural form of marketing for Nomad List and future nomad products.
- His conclusion: build an engaging community from day one. It improves engagement, supports real-time user research, and the Nomad List user tail "goes up again".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Levels reflects on self-releasing his 2008 drum & bass album, building and marketing everything himself. He concludes that marketing can take you far, but time is better spent making the product great, and that gatekeepers and tastemakers still matter.

chunks.heading: Great products push themselves; marketing alone has limits
chunks.text:
- Pieter's core claim: "Make a great product. Chances are it will push itself before you even thought about marketing it."
- Marketing and putting a product on the market yourself "can get you far, but an absolutely great product pushes itself."
- He applies this beyond music, to products in general.
- Self-assessment of his own album: it was a great product, "but it could be a lot better." He believes that if he had put the time he spent on marketing and promotion into making the music better, it would have gone much further.
- You can market something to success, but "you can not force people to like" it.

chunks.heading: What the 2008 drum & bass album project involved
chunks.text:
Pieter released a 12-track drum & bass album in 2008 and did everything himself:

- Music, mixing and mastering.
- Artwork.
- Writing the payment processing system.
- All promotion, plus folding posters.
- Becoming a publisher to collect royalties.
- Fulfilment: putting CDs into envelopes and cycling to the post office every week to send new orders.
- Result: he sold the entire batch of 1000 CDs and 2000 posters, all over the internet.
- He had an amazing time and calls independent release "a crazy experience."
- The campaign site was retakemanhattan.com, with a tongue-in-cheek pitch that the Dutch would "retake Manhattan" (New Amsterdam became New York).
- The project spun off into a very popular YouTube channel, the Panda Mix Show.

chunks.heading: You can't do everything alone, even when you can
chunks.text:
- Pieter's lesson: "to be successful in music, you cannot do everything on your own. And even if you can, you don't want to."
- You will always need others, such as tastemakers and big DJs who push your name. The internet has not changed that.
- He argues he could have benefited from earning the respect of those people before releasing his own album. He did some of this, but not enough.

chunks.heading: Distribution comes from tastemakers, not labels
chunks.text:
His advice to musicians:

- Be stubborn and do your own thing.
- Don't rely on labels to push you.
- Do rely on tastemakers, such as DJs or niche YouTube channels, to push you.
- People want to see you pushed up by significant people in a genre's scene before you go your own way.
- Significant people will find you when you make good music: "They will."

chunks.heading: Get good before you launch independently
chunks.text:
- Don't release your own work independently too early.
- Get really good at the craft first.
- "Great music is like valuable information, it wants to be free and it will at some point."
- Priority order he implies: quality first, then endorsement from respected people in the niche, then self-release and marketing.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A one-line essay arguing that building a product in secret, without letting people use it early, is the surest path to making something nobody wants. The implicit lesson is to ship early and get real users on it fast so feedback shapes the product.

chunks.heading: Building in the dark produces products nobody wants
chunks.text:
Pieter's core claim, posted on 13 October 2021, is that "Building a product in the dark without letting people use it early on is the best way to make something nobody wants."

- The failure mode is building privately, with no real users touching the product in the early stages.
- He frames this as the most reliable route to a product with no demand, not as one risk among many.
- The post is tagged Entrepreneurship, Analysis and Creativity on levels.io.

chunks.heading: Early usage is the safeguard
chunks.text:
The inverse of the claim is the practical rule: let people use the product early.

- Pieter's wording is "letting people use it early on", so the emphasis is on actual use, not just showing the product or collecting opinions.
- Early use is what separates a product people want from one built in isolation.
- The word "early" matters. The problem is delaying contact with users until the product is already built.

chunks.heading: Who this applies to
chunks.text:
The post is addressed to anyone building a startup or product, including solo makers. Pieter links his book MAKE, about building startups without funding, as the broader context for this advice.

- The principle is general: it is not tied to one product type or channel.
- The source gives no specific tactics, numbers or examples for how to release early. It states the principle only.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Pieter Levels argues that the cost of starting a startup has collapsed. A cheap laptop, free tutorials, a $0.99 domain and a $2.49/mo server are enough to begin, so lack of resources is no longer a valid excuse.

chunks.heading: The 2018 cost floor for starting a startup
chunks.text:
Pieter argues that barriers to starting a startup had "never been so low" as of July 2018. He backs this with four concrete cost points:

- Laptop: a Chromebook costs $149.
- Learning: YouTube has free code tutorials.
- Domain: a domain name costs $0.99/year.
- Hosting: a VPS server costs $2.49/month.

His point is that money and access are no longer valid excuses. The total outlay to get a first product online is small enough that cost is not the real obstacle.

chunks.heading: The "what are you waiting for?" mindset
chunks.text:
Pieter closes the argument with a challenge: "What are you waiting for?" He frames hesitation, not resources, as the remaining barrier.

- Tools, education, infrastructure and distribution channels are cheap or free.
- Waiting for funding, a better setup or permission is treated as avoidable delay.
- The implied action is to start building now with the cheapest available stack.

chunks.heading: Bootstrapping without funding
chunks.text:
Pieter ties the argument to his book MAKE, which he describes as being about "building startups without funding." The low costs above are the practical basis for that approach:

- A bootstrapped founder needs no investor money to cover a laptop, a domain and a small server.
- Ongoing costs are low enough (a couple of dollars a month for hosting) that a project can run indefinitely while it finds traction.
- Keeping costs near zero removes the pressure to raise capital before validating an idea.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A short emoji-based essay contrasting the emotional trajectories of VC-funded and bootstrapped startups. VC startups start with a rush of money and euphoria that ends in a crash, while bootstrapped startups start with doubt and struggle before ending in sustained happiness.

chunks.heading: The emoji timeline: VC startups vs bootstrapped startups
chunks.text:
Pieter compares the two paths in emoji, a 2017 post that reached roughly 1,047,801 views, 4,497 likes and 1,747 reposts.

- VC startups: 💰 then ten 😁 (up to 😁😁😁😁😁😁😁😁😁), then 🔥💥 and finally 😫😫😫.
- Bootstrapped startups: 🤔🤓😮😧😵😞😒 then 💰 then 😏🙂😀😄😃😆😁.

chunks.heading: What the VC path looks like in his telling
chunks.text:
- The money (💰) arrives first, at the very start.
- A long stretch of excitement and success feelings follows the funding.
- It ends in 🔥💥 (a blow-up or crash) and then three stressed faces (😫😫😫), meaning the pain comes last.
- Pieter's point: the high is front-loaded and the stress and burnout come at the end.

chunks.heading: What the bootstrapped path looks like in his telling
chunks.text:
- It starts with thinking and tinkering (🤔🤓), then shock, worry, confusion and disappointment (😮😧😵😞😒).
- The money (💰) only arrives after that rough early stretch.
- After the money, the emotions climb steadily through smiling and laughing faces to a wide grin (😏🙂😀😄😃😆😁).
- Pieter's point: the pain is front-loaded and the payoff, in money and mood, comes at the end.

chunks.heading: The core takeaway
chunks.text:
- The same ingredients (money and emotions) appear in both paths, but in reverse order.
- VC: cash first, then fun, then crash and stress.
- Bootstrapped: struggle first, then cash, then lasting happiness.
- This frames bootstrapping as the path Pieter prefers. He promotes his book MAKE as being about "building startups without funding".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Levels uses Carta median data to show how each funding round and each co-founder shrinks a founder's stake, then converts that into expected payouts at a $1B exit, a median $71M exit, and probability-weighted outcomes. His point: VC is a moonshot game, and the typical founder ends with a small slice of a small exit.

chunks.heading: How VC funding dilutes founder ownership by round
chunks.text:
Pieter's core point: raising money is not free. "People don't give you money out of charity, they buy a little slice of your company every time they invest." Each round sells a share of ownership in exchange for cash, in the hope that the founder's smaller slice becomes worth more than the ownership given away.

He argues ~5% is probably the most common final stake for VC-funded founders when things work out, especially with a co-founder.

chunks.heading: Median founder ownership by round (data via Carta)
chunks.text:
**Single founder:**
- Seed: ~56%
- Series A: ~36%
- Series B: ~23.5%
- Series C: ~16.5%
- Series D: ~10%
- Series E: <10%

**One co-founder (most startups):**
- Seed: ~28%
- Series A: ~18%
- Series B: ~11.75%
- Series C: ~8.25%
- Series D: ~5%
- Series E: <5%

**One of 4 co-founders:**
- Seed: ~14%
- Series A: ~9%
- Series B: ~5.875%
- Series C: ~4.125%
- Series D: ~2.5%
- Series E: <2.5%

chunks.heading: Payout at a $1 billion acquisition
chunks.text:
Pieter runs the same stakes against a $1B exit ("$1 billion is a lot!").

- **Single founder:** Seed ~$560M, Series A ~$360M, Series B ~$235M, Series C ~$165M, Series D ~$100M, Series E <$100M.
- **One co-founder:** Seed ~$280M, Series A ~$180M, Series B ~$117.5M, Series C ~$82.5M, Series D ~$50M, Series E <$50M.
- **One of 4 co-founders:** Seed ~$140M, Series A ~$90M, Series B ~$59M, Series C ~$41M, Series D ~$25M, Series E <$25M.

chunks.heading: Payout at the realistic median acquisition (~$71M)
chunks.text:
The median acquisition value for a VC-backed startup sits at approximately $71 million.

- **Single founder:** Seed ~$39.8M, Series A ~$25.6M, Series B ~$16.7M, Series C ~$11.7M, Series D ~$7.1M, Series E <$7.1M.
- **One co-founder:** Seed ~$19.9M, Series A ~$12.8M, Series B ~$8.3M, Series C ~$5.9M, Series D ~$3.55M, Series E <$3.55M.
- **One of 4 co-founders:** Seed ~$9.95M, Series A ~$6.4M, Series B ~$4.2M, Series C ~$2.9M, Series D ~$1.8M, Series E <$1.8M.

chunks.heading: Median expected outcome, with acquisition probability included
chunks.text:
Two inputs: the median acquisition happens around Series A (quite early), and the median acquisition value is $71M. That gives the median outcome for a startup that does get acquired:

- Single founder: ~$25.6M
- One co-founder: ~$12.8M
- One of 4 co-founders: ~$6.4M

But "most startups are by definition doomed to fail," and only ~15% ever get acquired. Weighting by that probability:

- Single founder: ~$3.84M
- One of two co-founders: ~$1.92M
- One of four co-founders: ~$960,000

chunks.heading: Caveats and how Pieter frames it
chunks.text:
- The numbers ignore taxes and liquidation preferences. Investors may be paid their preference before common shareholders receive anything, so founders would get even less.
- They also ignore founders taking money off the table in earlier rounds. Pieter says the two omissions "balance each other out a bit."
- He is not calling VC bad: "it's just how the VC game works but good to write it out and be aware of how it works."
- VC-backed startups "shoot for the moon." It is one of the few ways to get a crazy big payout and become an actual billionaire, which he says is very rare for a bootstrapped founder using their own money.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Levels argues indie hacking, which got big around 2016, has completed a 7-year cycle and been absorbed into mainstream startup thinking. It effectively updated the Lean Startup: skip customer interviews, prototype fast, launch, kill what fails, and market by building in public.

chunks.heading: Indie hacking's 2016-2023 cycle and why it "died"
chunks.text:
- Pieter says indie hacking got big around 2016 and, on his 7-year cycle theory, was due to die by 2023. The post is headlined "R.I.P. Indie hacking, 2016 - 2023".
- His reading of the "death" is not failure. Indie hacking became "part of the normal, the status quo".
- Its principles are now something "any startup founder's mindset" will "at least consider".

chunks.heading: Indie hacking as the successor to the Lean Startup
chunks.text:
- Pieter argues indie hacking has "replaced the Lean Startup of 2010", as an update to it.
- The key change is skipping customer interviews. Founders go "straight to lean prototyping".

chunks.heading: The indie hacker playbook, as Pieter summarizes it
chunks.text:
- Launch fast.
- "Throw stuff at the wall and see what sticks."
- "Nuke it if it doesn't work" and go on to the next project.
- Broadcast the journey publicly and use that as marketing.

chunks.heading: Distribution through building in public
chunks.text:
- In this model, public broadcasting of the journey is the marketing channel. There is no separate marketing budget or campaign.
- Each project launched and shut down publicly feeds an audience that carries over to the next project.

chunks.heading: The next generation of founders
chunks.text:
- Pieter says new Gen Z founders are "indie hackers and nomads by default".
- They are also open to raising funding later, so indie hacking and venture funding are no longer opposites.
- Bootstrapping first and raising later has become a normal path rather than a rejection of funding.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Levels shares a friend's report from an indie hacker meetup: builders obsess over code-generating systems and agent pipelines while lacking customers, revenue, and any idea where to get traffic. The post frames AI-era building as a comfortable way to avoid marketing and distribution.

chunks.heading: Pieter's observation: indie hackers over-build and under-distribute
chunks.text:
- Pieter shares a friend's report from an indie hacker meetup in June 2026. Almost everyone there was "super focused on development."
- They built "whole spaceships" that generate code, review it and produce reports and analytics.
- One attendee built an entire "factory": a list of ideas, with agents generating the landing page, the SaaS and the analytics, all pulled into one dashboard.
- The builders optimized all of it heavily and were comfortable doing so.

chunks.heading: The core problem: no money and no traffic
chunks.text:
- The friend's key finding, which Pieter amplifies: "almost none of them have money or traffic."
- Nobody at the meetup knew where to get either one.
- Building is the comfortable part, so people keep polishing the system instead of facing marketing.
- The result is a lot of output with no audience and no revenue.

chunks.heading: Procrastination pattern: "marketing later, after my system is done"
chunks.text:
- A common line from these builders: "yeah, I should probably do marketing, but first I'll finish my super system and then I'll start."
- The marketing plan is often just another automation project, such as building an agent that posts to Instagram automatically.
- This repeats the old trap in a new form. Marketing gets postponed behind more tooling, and tooling becomes a way to avoid talking to customers.

chunks.heading: AI makes the old programmer mistake worse
chunks.text:
- Pieter and his friend compare this to the classic programmer, who spent a year writing code and tests and preparing for scale "in the basement" without showing anything to anyone.
- Their view is that it is now worse: "the amount of useless aislop nobody needs has grown massively."
- Because AI lets anyone build, building is no longer the differentiator.

chunks.heading: Takeaway: distribution is the real challenge
chunks.text:
- Pieter links this to his related post "Everyone can now build apps with AI so now distribution is the real challenge."
- The principle: when building is cheap, the scarce resource is traffic and paying customers, not code or automation infrastructure.
- Automated idea-to-SaaS pipelines, code-review systems and dashboards do not solve the question of where users and money come from.
- Priority should go to showing the product to people and finding a source of traffic and revenue, rather than perfecting internal systems first.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A one-line post from Pieter Levels observing that with AI-assisted coding, building speed now outpaces idea generation. It signals a shift in the bottleneck for solo makers from execution to ideation.

chunks.heading: Pieter builds faster than he gets new ideas
chunks.text:
- Pieter says it is "such a weird experience" that he can now build things faster than he gets new ideas for things to build.
- The bottleneck has flipped. Building used to be the slow, scarce step, and ideas were the cheap part. Now building is cheap and fast, and good ideas are the limiting factor.
- He ties this to AI and vibe coding (the post is tagged AI, Creativity, Entrepreneurship and Vibe Coding).
- Posted 2 October 2026 on X, where it drew 153,621 views, 4,423 likes and 174 reposts.

chunks.heading: Implication for builders
chunks.text:
- Pieter's framing implies that if building cost is no longer the constraint, the scarce skill is coming up with ideas worth building.
- He states only the observation. The source gives no tactics, numbers, tools, or advice on how to generate ideas.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Levels received a $45K offer for his second 12-startups-in-12-months project after one month of work. He declined because the price didn't reflect the site's potential, he was still enjoying it, and he wants to build startups rather than cash out cheaply. He also lists his five goals for the experiment.

chunks.heading: Pieter's decision framework for a $45K acquisition offer on Go Fucking Do It
chunks.text:
In June 2014, during his "12 startups in 12 months" challenge, Pieter received his first offer to buy one of his startups, Go Fucking Do It (gofuckingdoit.com), his second project of the series. The buyer opened with interest and, when asked for a price range, named $45,000.

- The final offer was $45,000, about EUR 33,000.
- Dutch tax would take 52%, leaving him about EUR 16,000.
- The site had only been about a month of work, and he found the experience of being asked "kinda excited" and "very flattering".
- He did not sell. He read the offer as a sign he was "on to something here that I can scale up".

chunks.heading: How he decided: price against the site's potential
chunks.text:
Pieter judged the offer against what the site could become, not against the effort already spent.

- His reasoning: if he can scale the site 10x, it could generate double the offer in annual revenue alone.
- Because of that, any sale would need to be "a strong multiple" of $45K before he would consider it.
- The offer felt too low for the site's potential even though it was well above the month of work invested.
- Tax mattered to the real number: a headline of EUR 33,000 became about EUR 16,000 after Dutch tax at 52%.

chunks.heading: Passion and freshness as a reason to keep building
chunks.text:
He also weighed how he felt about the project, not only the money.

- He was "having way too much fun with it still"; the concept and execution were "still so fresh" and did not bore him yet.
- Selling a project he still enjoys would trade a learning and growth opportunity for a modest payout.

chunks.heading: Why a small exit is a trap for a builder
chunks.text:
Pieter compared a sale to simply working for money as a freelancer.

- He noted that he is "trying to build startups here, not be just an expensive web developer (at EUR 16k/m)".
- Taking EUR 16k after tax for a month's work would pay like a high-priced contractor, which is the opposite of building assets that compound.
- His point: small exits turn a founder back into a service provider, selling time at a premium instead of owning something that scales.

chunks.heading: The five goals he uses to evaluate any offer
chunks.text:
The offer made him write down what 12 startups in 12 months is actually for. In order:

1. Have lots of fun and learn startup development and marketing.
2. Meet lots of interesting people in the startup world (which he already had).
3. Maintain his living standards with his projects without needing a job.
4. Attract investment for one project and work with a team to scale something to 1M in revenue.
5. Sell one project for an actual good amount of money, giving a few years of runway and financial independence to build new things while traveling.

An offer only makes sense if it advances these goals. A $45K sale funded about a year of living but ended a project that could serve goals 3 and 4.

chunks.heading: What he took away and did next
chunks.text:
- Being asked to sell was validation that the project had real value and could be scaled.
- His response was to double down: his closing line was "let's go fucking grow it", pointing to a public challenge on his own site, "Grow my startup", with a 2015-01-01 deadline.
- He treated the offer as a signal to grow rather than as an exit, and kept the option of a sale later at a much better multiple.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A one-line essay from Pieter Levels on idea generation: open the Craigslist front page and pick an item category that you could build a company around. It frames existing marketplaces as a ready-made source of validated demand.

chunks.heading: Craigslist front page as a startup idea generator
chunks.text:
Pieter's tactic for finding a startup idea is to go to the Craigslist front page and pick an item you can build a company around. The front page lists categories of real things people already buy, sell, hire for and look for, so it works as a ready-made list of proven markets.

- The method is simple. Browse the Craigslist front page and find an item or category that you could turn into a standalone company.
- The idea comes from existing demand, not from inventing a problem yourself.
- The implied step is to build a focused, better product around one slice of what Craigslist handles in a generic way (jobs, housing, services, for sale).

He shared this on 14 November 2018 as part of his advice on building startups without funding, the theme of his book MAKE.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Pieter Levels argues that indie businesses in 2018 benefit from declining trust in Big Tech, public affection for small businesses, and audiences who want to join the founder's journey. Those tailwinds make feedback and money easier to get when you build in the open.

chunks.heading: Why 2018 favors indie businesses over Big Tech
chunks.text:
Pieter argues that people forget how much structural advantage an indie business has in 2018. He names three tailwinds working in a small builder's favor:

- People no longer trust Big Tech companies.
- People love to support small businesses.
- People love to follow a founder's journey and be part of it.

chunks.heading: Trust as the opening against Big Tech
chunks.text:
- Pieter's first point is that distrust of Big Tech is now widespread ("People don't trust Big Tech companies anymore").
- The implication he draws is that an indie business starts with a positioning edge: it is the small, human, accountable alternative to a large company.
- He frames this as an advantage that is easy to overlook, not as something an indie has to build from scratch.

chunks.heading: Small business goodwill
chunks.text:
- Pieter says people actively "love to support small businesses."
- Being small and independent is therefore an asset in how customers decide who to buy from, not a handicap to hide.
- Founders can lean into being small rather than trying to look like a large company.

chunks.heading: Building in public: the audience as participants
chunks.text:
- Pieter says people "love to follow your journey and be part of it by helping you in any way (feedback, money)."
- The audience helps in two concrete ways he names: feedback and money.
- The journey itself works as a distribution and engagement asset. Sharing the story turns followers into contributors and customers.
- This is consistent with the approach of his book MAKE, about building startups without funding.
